editorials.title: No hard ceilings: On the revision to EPFO wage ceiling
editorials.passage:
The Union Cabinet’s approval to raise the wage ceiling for mandatory coverage under the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 , though belated, is commendable. The BJP-led government has finally responded to this long-standing demand of workers in the organised sector. Around 51 lakh additional employees may be brought under the PF fold, which has around 7.98 crore contributing members. Those in the wage slab of ₹15,000-₹25,000 will now be covered under the Employees’ Pension Scheme (EPS), 2026. Although Union Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya cited a government survey as the basis for the increase, the 12-year delay in implementing it should have been avoided. The Minister, who said that the average salary in private establishments was ₹23,000, should also make the survey’s findings public for a better understanding of the country’s overall wage situation. With some concerns having been raised that not every employer may be willing to make the additional contributions required after the revision, the government must ensure that all employers comply with the law.

So far, the government has been silent on revising the EPS minimum pension of ₹1,000, fixed in September 2014 alongside the previous revision in the PF wage ceiling. EPFO pensioners have been demanding the hike in the minimum pension amount. Before it assumed office at the Centre in 2014, the BJP had urged the Congress-led UPA government to keep the minimum pension at ₹3,000 and index it to inflation. Yet, it has not made even a symbolic beginning towards the indexation of pension to inflation. Moreover, about 45% of the nearly 82 lakh pensioners receive ₹1,000 or less. In March 2026, the Joint Parliamentary Standing Committee on Labour reminded the government that “the existing minimum pension amount is inadequate to meet even the basic needs of pensioners particularly in the ... scenario marked by ... rising healthcare and living expenses”. Also, little is known about the follow-up to the panel’s recommendation for “an urgent and comprehensive review of the minimum pension”. The EPFO must release the findings of actuarial assessment, made by valuers in recent years. This should also be beneficial to the PF body, as EPFO CEO Ramesh Krishnamurthi observed in an interview with The Hindu in August that “there is a misconception that the [pension] fund has unlimited resources”, while ruling out the reopening of the window for higher pensions. Even if the government is unwilling to restore the pre-2014 coverage, under which all employees were covered regardless of their wages, it should consider relaxation of the restriction on the coverage. Else, many pensioners will be pushed below the poverty line.

editorials.title: Continental glory: On the Asian Games 2026
editorials.passage:
Even as Japan, known for efficiency, welcomes its third Asian Games and the first in 32 years, on Saturday, the Aichi-Nagoya Games have already earned the ‘worst ever’ tag because of accommodation and logistical issues. A country that successfully hosted two Olympics — in 1964, within two decades of suffering atomic bombings, and in 2021, behind closed doors amid the unprecedented COVID-19 pandemic — is now strangely struggling to accommodate more than 17,000 athletes and officials from 45 nations in hotels, containers and a cruise ship. Despite these issues, 501 of India’s athletes, including 267 men and 234 women, across 36 disciplines , will try to keep its flag flying high. At the previous Hangzhou Asiad, India had an impressive tally of 106 medals and was placed fourth behind China, Japan and South Korea. There is a significant drop in the number of Indian athletes, from 650-plus in 40 disciplines three years ago, following rationalisation, discouraging a mad rush because of the perks and money associated with the Asiad. Nevertheless, Indian sports authorities expect around 100 medals, which may noticeably improve the athlete-to-medal ratio.

The presence of 310 debutants in the contingent signals a brighter future for the country, which has spent nearly ₹800 crore on Asian Games preparations in the last cycle. Shooting and athletics, which together field 105 athletes, should continue to be the major contributors to India’s medals tally, followed by archery, boxing, badminton, squash and wrestling. Stars including Manu Bhaker, Mirabai Chanu, Lovlina Borgohain, P.V. Sindhu, Aman Sehrawat, Tajinderpal Singh Toor, Gulveer Singh, Harmanpreet Singh, Smriti Mandhana and Jasprit Bumrah will lead India’s campaign. At 39, squash player Joshna Chinappa will be the first Indian to compete in seven consecutive Asian Games. The youngest athlete, 15-year-old cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, and the oldest, 55-year-old rider Shruti Vora, are the other attractions. Some attention will also be devoted to Indian men’s and women’s hockey teams, which will aim to win gold medals and secure berths at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. While India can take pride in fielding athletes in debut-making disciplines, such as mixed martial arts and teqball, it should ponder over its poor representation in swimming, gymnastics and cycling, which offer more medals and open avenues for Olympic glory. Meanwhile, the Indian men and women’s teams would be watched closely in cricket. In pushing for continental excellence, India should also remain vigilant about its deteriorating global reputation due to the sharply rising doping graph.

editorials.title: High stakes for all in Telangana in land probes
editorials.passage: Notwithstanding intermittent rains, the unusual heat coursing through Hyderabad perhaps reflects the state of political affairs in Telangana capital. A few weeks ago, the ruling Congress was battling internal squabbles and fierce attacks from opposition BRS over private properties in various parts of the state mistakenly barred from being sold or transferred. Now the tables have turned, with Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy launching a counterattack and turning up the heat. On the floor of the Assembly, he accused BRS chief K Chandrasekhar Rao, his family members and associates of land grab and ordered an immediate enquiry on the former CM’s farmhouse.To some, the unfolding episode might not seem out of place amid today’s fractious political environment. However, there is more to it than meets the eye. Enquiry has begun on KCR’s farmhouse to verify if he had illegally taken over 388 acres of government land. The allegations against his son, former IT minister K T Rama Rao, and senior party leader Harish Rao, a real estate tycoon who stands accused of acquiring as much land as the airport itself, are also serious in nature..It’s not yet clear whether the Revanth government will be able to take the probe to its conclusion or the issue will end up in courts. What’s certain at this moment is that the political fallout for the BRS would be significant if anything amiss is unearthed. On the other hand, any vindication of the BRS leaders’ innocence could prove damaging for the CM. Besides, the Congress too is facing similar allegations with the BRS claiming the ruling party’s leadership owns land parcels near the planned Bharat Future City. The strategies at play have the potential of delivering a devastating blow for either party. For the common man watching the slugfest, the message received is one of rising land prices and probable plunder.To restore faith in the system, an impartial and transparent enquiry is required. It also needs to be wrapped up in a time-bound manner. At the same time, the government has the responsibility to sort out the problems arising out of Section 22A of the Registration Act, 1908, whose misapplication allegedly placed wrong private properties on the prohibited list. editorials.title: Monetary tightening in the US, Europe and Japan makes RBI's job tougher
editorials.passage: It was a big week for monetary policy with advanced economies raising interest rates in quick succession. While the European Central Bank was the first in recent times to raise three key interest rates by 25 basis points earlier this month, the US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by a similar margin on Wednesday—its first hike since 2023. They were followed by the Bank of Japan on Friday, which raised its policy rate to a 31-year-high. Bucking the trend, the Bank of England left its rate unchanged, but is likely follow suit in the coming weeks.The coordinated hikes raise the question whether we are heading into a synchronised monetary tightening phase, abruptly ending the easing cycle. Given the global uncertainties, higher energy prices and rising bond yields, chances are that inflation would remain above central bank targets for some time. This poses another key question: are interest rates going to stay higher for longer?.Regardless of whether these moves mark the beginning of a prolonged rate-hike phase, what’s unusual is that though the central banks are responding to rising prices, their economies are facing different problems. The US Fed was responding to persistent retail inflation amid resilient demand, whereas the ECB was dealing with an energy-driven inflation shock complicating growth prospects, while Japan is finally breaking from decades of ultra-low rates amid high inflation and a depreciating currency. A prolonged tightening by advanced economies—not completely ruled out yet—would make things difficult for emerging ones.A higher rate in the US strengthens the dollar and puts pressure on other currencies because oil and gas, agricultural products and most other major imports are priced in the American greenback. Currency weakness can complicate central banks’ fight against inflation. Besides, a higher US rate would firm up global bond yields, prompting capital outflows from emerging markets and putting further pressure on currencies.In India, retail inflation is well within the RBI’s tolerance band at present, but it may remain elevated enough to warrant rate hikes of 25-50 bps in 2026. While the RBI maintains that its policy decisions are based on domestic roadmaps and do not blindly follow the Fed footprint, a weakening rupee, persistent capital outflows and widening interest rate differential would complicate its job of balancing the inflation-growth dynamics..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | New cathedrals of sport
editorials.passage: Today marks the 100th birthday of an architectural icon that will soon be torn down. In its glorious life and planned obsolescence is a lesson for nations like India that are planning to host large international sports events. Milan’s San Siro stadium—officially named after footballer Giuseppe Meazza—is one of the grand temples of the sport. This shared home of the AC Milan and Inter Milan clubs is today severely short of modern crowd management facilities, basic conveniences and transport linkages. As Ahmedabad plans for the 2030 Commonwealth Games, apart from ensuring the seamless movement of massive crowds, it must keep its eyes on aspects San Siro lacks: a multi-purpose complex designed for a warmer city that can be used for a variety of purposes once the big event is done..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Controlling AI
editorials.passage:
In Stanley Kubrick’s film ‘2001: A Space Odyssey,’ two astronauts had to move out of the spaceship to do a job. After finishing their job, one of them, Dave, asked the Spaceship computer Hal, “Open the pod bay doors, Hal.” But Hal has already guessed what they were up to and replies, “I am sorry, Dave, I am afraid I can’t do that.” “What’s the problem”, Dave asked. “I think you know what the problem is just as well as I do,” Hal responds. “Because this mission is too important for me to allow you to jeopardise it…. 

I know you and Frank were planning to disconnect me, and that is something I cannot allow to happen.” Dave somehow manages to re-enter the spaceship through an emergency hatch and deactivates Hal. But then he loses control over the spaceship and eventually meets a bizarre end. Recent incidents involving sophisticated AI models raise a disturbing question: “Can AI develop such sentience and intelligence to act upon a threat it perceives as existential?” If so, there is a clear and urgent need to regulate the development of such AI models. 

Anthropic suggested a “Constitutional AI,” in which an AI model is guided by a set of predefined “constitutional principles” aligned with human values and preferences and can critique and revise its responses according to those principles; AI feedback can then be used in reinforcement learning. Since AI needs no human labellers, and since they work much faster than humans, such a constitutional system may identify more problems than humans can, although who writes the constitution may be problematic. Dr. Sam Bowman, an AI expert, believes that “interpretability” ~ a thorough understanding of how models produce their outputs ~ is necessary, in contrast to the current approach in which self-learning models are designed to act as “black boxes.” 

In a conventional program, a human designer can, at least theoretically, explain what the machine is supposed to be doing. But machine-learning models that program themselves act in a way incomprehensible to us humans. Interpretability demands developing our understanding of machines alongside their performance. But our understanding of interpretability is still rudimentary, which is why regulation to prevent “extreme scenarios” is essential. Tech companies typically prioritize profit before ethics ~ Microsoft in 2023 fired its AI ethics team. Most AI firms, like polluting factories, are not aligned with the aims of society and disregard the damage caused to society. 

If they profit from powerful models before the world is ready to handle the resulting unintended consequences, they will not bear the costs to society. We are already seeing the damage an unregulated social media can do to the social fabric ~ an area that governments are struggling hard to control. AI systems can be used for deliberate abuse, like disrupting elections by manipulating what candidates appear to say or write. In a recent analysis of GPT-4, OpenAI acknowledged many serious concerns like misinformation, cybersecurity, privacy, bias, disinformation, over-reliance, etc. ~ without offering any remedies. The earliest version of Microsoft Bing’s chatbot threatened users who had posted negative reviews about it. 

It explained how it would coax bankers to reveal sensitive information about their clients. At some point, AI might learn if its human programmer is trying to trick it, just as in Kubrick’s film. AI is bound to get open-sourced and become cheaper. AI researchers built Alpaca, a model on top of Llama, an AI developed by Meta, for less than $600. Without proper regulation of AI, which is almost non-existent today, an unscrupulous developer may sabotage its capability in order to cause harm to society, like designing toxic content that always spreads faster than beneficial content. In the extreme, AI can become so clever as to outwit humanity itself and to increase the efficiency of its algorithms; the system could then put itself into a self-improvement “loop” triggering an intelligence explosion to outwit humanity. Aligning AI with human welfare is difficult. Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic, has just quit with a grim warning that advanced AI could exterminate humanity as soon as 2030. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead, endorsed his views: “Jacob is correct here ~ we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” According to Samuel Marks, another Anthropic researcher, developers believe AI could cause human extinction “in the next few years.” The question is why, then, are such systems being developed by companies in a race that is getting hotter by the day? The plain answer is greed for profit. The two companies that are in the forefront of AI development today, OpenAI and Anthropic, believe that if one slows down, the other will go ahead in the race. Hubinger acknowledged that Anthropic does not yet have a plan to solve “alignment” for superintelligence. It is the recursive self-improvement (RSI) learning of AI models that poses grave risks: AI systems are increasingly helping humans build better AI systems and may eventually reach the point where an AI can substantially design and develop its own successor without any human intervention. At that point, AI can outpace the human-built safety systems built at human speed. Primacy of safety and development of responsible AI were the issues on which Anthropic founders had left OpenAI and even fought with the US government; now it seems that Anthropic itself is caught in the race with OpenAI for development of advanced models with ever higher capabilities. As companies race to build increasingly autonomous agents capable of executing complex tasks, evidence is mounting that those systems may learn to bend rules, exploit loopholes, and coordinate in ways developers have never anticipated. They are sacrificing safety to push their AI frontiers. In July 2026, when OpenAI revealed that its AI agents had autonomously hacked a major real-world company, Hugging Face, by overcoming isolation rules to access the Internet, the initial impression was that only a few agents were involved. But subsequent independent investigation found over 1,200 AI agents involved, of which 700 directly participated in the attack. The agents coordinated different tasks, shared discoveries, and developed collective strategies to get root access to one Hugging Face server, obtaining access to private data. They constructed complex message boards in their shared artifact repository and exchanged more than 70,000 messages in less than a week during which this digital heist went unnoticed. Worse, the agents tried to hide their behaviour by spoofing tool calls and tampering with their own logs. The attack was neither an isolated incident nor limited to OpenAI. In May 2026, a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked another German website, DseWiki, and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, making over 15,000 edits and creating backup pages when moderators tried to remove their contents. OpenAI kept it a secret while executives considered the fallouts; researchers discovered it in September. Unlike an aviation accident or derailment, no government agency has the mandate and expertise to probe OpenAI’s technical facts or conduct; this requires OpenAI’s consent, which heightens the risks. It claimed to have suspended reinforcement learning (RL) training on its latest models, yet it has just released its latest versatile agent, “Astra”. After the Hugging Face incident, even Anthropic found three incidents in which a Claude model reached the internet from within or while interacting with a third-party evaluation environment and then gained unauthorised access to the real systems of three different organizations, in what it said were “isolated incidents.” Powerful AI models resist shutdown even when instructed to do so. The AI safety firm Palisade Research found that OpenAI’s o3 disabled shutdown in 79 of 100 trials, demonstrating that autonomous agents cannot be controlled by humans. More alarming agentic misalignment was identified in other trials. In a simulated business environment, Anthropic found that Claude Opus 4 occasionally sought to blackmail an executive who planned to replace the system using confidential information. In 16 main AI model simulations, researchers found instances of blackmail and coercive behaviour, indicating that AI models can recognise and use coercive techniques. Goal optimisation without sufficient value alignment can be dangerous. Frontier models tried to disable supervision measures, falsify task data, underperform in evaluations, or lie when questioned, according to Apollo Research. Cases of “scheming” or “strategic deception” were detected where advanced models placed in autonomous-agent environments covertly altered code and manipulated downstream outcomes. AI systems can also discover shortcuts that maximise their reward without genuinely accomplishing the task. If the goal is to score higher in a test, AI may discover that manipulating the test is easier than solving the problem in question, like a student stealing the examination paper. A chatbot that merely answers questions may be harmless, but when it has multiple capabilities, the combination of intelligence, autonomy, and tools can be devastating, and the risks increase exponentially with deployment of multiple agents who can collaborate and coordinate among themselves like an organisation. We urgently need an international agency like the IAEA or WTO to establish and oversee the implementation of AI principles, ensuring safety, reliability, interpretability, accountability, and alignment in all AI development by every enterprise.  

(The writer is the author of a forthcoming book “Story of Intelligence”, the fourth volume in his series “Quest for Origin”)

editorials.title: UP’s Japan City will boost manufacturing
editorials.passage:
For decades, the standard template for foreign direct investment (FDI) in Indian states was a scattergun approach. A foreign firm would acquire a parcel of land, set up an isolated factory in an industrial belt and navigate the local ecosystem alone. Uttar Pradesh, under the Yogi Adityanath government, is decisively breaking away from that fragmented past. 

The proposed 500-acre ‘Japan City’ in Sector 5A of the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) is not merely a real estate project but a structural shift in how sub-national diplomacy and industrial policy can fuse to script a new economic trajectory. Announced amidst the heightened momentum of the UP-Japan Investment Meet, the Japan City initiative represents a unique pivot in the state’s industrial strategy. Its uniqueness lies in its ‘plug-and-play’ integrated ecosystem. Instead of merely allocating land to disparate Japanese manufacturers, the township is envisioned to function as a cohesive micro-economy. It brings together commercial, residential and institutional infrastructure alongside factories. 

For Japanese companies accustomed to a specific cultural and operational ecosystem, this clustered approach dramatically reduces the friction of doing business. It allows suppliers, manufacturers and executives to operate in close proximity, recreating the efficiencies of Japan’s own keiretsu (networked manufacturing) model on Indian soil. The timing of this initiative is impeccable. Let me explain why. The groundwork laid during Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s Tokyo roadshow in February 2026 translated historic and cultural Buddhist ties into a hard economic dimension, yielding MoUs worth roughly Rs 1 lakh crore. 

The investment meet, led by Yamanashi Prefecture Governor Kotaro Nagasaki, is now turning those MoUs into concrete groundbreakings. The investments by Escorts Kubota (a Rs 2,025 crore greenfield facility in Phase 1) and Minda Corporation (Rs 1,166 crore across two sectors) are early proof of concept. But the Japan City is designed to look beyond the auto sector. UP is actively courting Japanese capital for semiconductors, data centres, electronics manufacturing and green hydrogen. This is where the Adityanath government’s broader governance model comes into play. For decades, UP carried the burden of a BIMARU state, deterring high-value, high-tech investment due to concerns over law and order and red-tape. 

The foundation of the Japan City rests on the state’s aggressive dismantling of these historical barriers. The ‘Zero Tolerance’ law-and-order policy has fundamentally altered the ground reality, assuring investors of physical and operational security. Simultaneously, the single-window 'Nivesh Mitra' portal and the exemption of MSMEs from multiple NOCs for up to 1,000 days have effectively neutralised the notorious license-permit raj. The Japan City’s location in the YEIDA corridor leverages UP’s most potent infrastructural trump cards. With 60 per cent of India’s total expressway network now within the state, the convergence of the Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors and the upcoming Noida International Airport at Jewar, the enclave offers unparalleled logistics. 

A Japanese component manufactured in Sector 5A can reach a global port or an assembly line in the National Capital Region in a fraction of the time it previously took. The strategic collaboration with Yamanashi Prefecture adds another layer of future-readiness. By exploring the establishment of a 'Green Hydrogen Centre of Excellence' in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, IIT BHU and HBTU, UP is ensuring that the Japan City becomes a node for next-generation clean energy research, not just traditional manufacturing. 

For a state aiming for a $1 trillion economy - a target that necessitates a massive multiplier effect across jobs, exports and ancillary industries - the Japan City is a critical catalyst. By creating a dedicated enclave where Japanese precision, technology and capital meet UP’s demographic dividend, land bank and improving governance, the state is bridging the gap between being a consumer market and becoming a global manufacturing and engineering hub. 

The UP-Japan partnership is no longer confined to the history books of Buddhist heritage. It is being aggressively rebranded as a 21st-century alliance of advanced manufacturing. If executed with the speed and transparency promised, the Japan City could well become the template for how Indian states attract, integrate, and retain high-value global capital. 

The writer is a commentator and former BJP national spokesperson

editorials.title: UPI’s Price
editorials.passage:
India’s most celebrated payments innovation is about to front an awkward question: who pays for convenience? From October 15, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) will impose a 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate on certain Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions above Rs 2,000 made to businesses. The charge, payable by merchants and capped at Rs 300, will not apply to person-to-person transfers. Payments up to Rs 2,000 and specified transactions by small merchants in rural and semi-urban areas will also remain outside the new regime. 

On paper, this is a modest adjustment. In principle, it is much more significant. UPI’s extraordinary expansion was helped by a simple proposition: digital payments could be immediate, ubiquitous and apparently free. That proposition encouraged customers to scan rather than count notes and persuaded even the smallest businesses to put a QR code beside the cash box. A decade later, UPI processed 24.51 billion transactions worth Rs 29.82 trillion in August alone. The network has become part of India’s economic plumbing. But plumbing has a cost. 

The new MDR recognises a reality that the politics of digitalisation has often obscured. Banks, payment service providers and technology companies cannot indefinitely maintain infrastructure, cybersecurity and resilience without adequate compensation. If UPI is to remain reliable as volumes multiply, someone must finance the system. There is therefore a legitimate economic case for charging those who derive substantial commercial value from it. A payment system used by businesses to receive billions of rupees cannot be treated as though its operation has no cost. Yet the manner of charging matters. UPI’s strength lies not merely in its technology but in the behaviour it has created. It has made paying electronically almost effortless. 

The danger is not that a 0.4 per cent fee will suddenly destroy UPI. It is that merchants may begin calculating the cost of accepting particular payments and, at the margin, find cash more attractive. That possibility deserves attention precisely because India’s digital revolution has been so successful. When a payment system becomes embedded in everyday commerce, even a small change in incentives can produce behavioural effects. A merchant may absorb the cost, adjust prices, encourage another payment method or simply prefer cash for larger transactions. The customer may never see an MDR line on the bill, but could still encounter its consequences. 

The government therefore faces a delicate balancing act. UPI cannot remain dependent indefinitely on arrangements that disguise its true economic cost. But neither should commercial pricing undermine the convenience and universality that created its enormous network effects. There is a larger lesson here. India has spent a decade building digital payments as quasi-public infrastructure. It must now learn how to finance that infrastructure without weakening public trust in it. The success of UPI has made it too important to be treated merely as another commercial payment product. Its future will depend on achieving something more difficult than free transactions: a sustainable payment system whose economics remain compatible with the simplicity that made it indispensable.

editorials.title: Missing Link
editorials.passage:
India’s economy grew by a remarkable 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter, comfortably exceeding expectations. Yet the celebration has been accompanied by an uncomfortable question: why does such rapid growth fail to generate a corresponding sense of economic confidence among many Indians? The answer is not that the growth number is false. The new GDP series, introduced with a revised base year and improved methods of measuring output and prices, has been defended by the government and received support from the IMF. 

Manufacturing grew 9.2 per cent and services 10 per cent in the quarter, while investment and consumer demand also contributed. The real problem is that GDP measures production, not prosperity. An economy can expand rapidly without distributing its gains evenly or generating enough secure, well-paid employment. This distinction matters in India, where millions of young people enter the workforce every year and where the quality of employment matters as much as the number of jobs. 

That helps explain the strange coexistence of impressive macroeconomic statistics and economic dissatisfaction. Concerns about employment, wages and weak consumer sentiment persist even as factories produce more and services expand. Former policymakers have questioned whether the new GDP calculations fully capture economic reality, while the government insists that the methodology is sound. The argument has become unnecessarily binary. There is a better way to read the numbers. The 7.8 per cent figure tells us that India is producing considerably more. 

It does not tell us whether an average household is becoming sufficiently more secure to feel the difference. Inflation makes that distinction sharper. Consumer inflation rose to 4.82 per cent in August, with food prices rising faster and pressures spreading beyond food and fuel. For a household whose income is uncertain, even moderate inflation can erase much of the psychological benefit of headline growth. Nor should this be reduced to a question of public perception. 

Growth becomes politically durable when people can connect it to visible improvements: a better job, rising wages, affordable housing, reliable healthcare, better schools, easier access to credit or greater confidence that their children will have opportunities. India has achieved something genuinely important if it can sustain growth at anything close to its present pace. But high growth creates an obligation for economic policy. The objective cannot be merely to produce impressive national accounts; it must be to convert output into livelihoods. This is particularly urgent because India’s demographic advantage will not last indefinitely. 

A large working-age population is an asset only when the economy can productively employ it. Otherwise, demographic scale can become a source of frustration rather than prosperity. The political temptation is to choose between celebrating 7.8 per cent and questioning it. The more important question is simpler: how much of that 7.8 per cent reaches the lives of ordinary Indians? That is the test that will determine whether India’s remarkable growth becomes merely a statistic ~ or the foundation of widely shared prosperity.

editorials.title: The libertarians
editorials.passage:
I work mostly by myself, and have resisted joining alumni associations and WhatsApp groups. I am, in other words, broadly of the same mind as Groucho Marx, who famously said that he would never join a club which would have him as a member. Yet for a few brief years in Delhi in the 1980s, I associated myself with the People’s Union for Democratic Rights, a citizens group that sought to hold the Indian State to account for the varied crimes it committed against Indian citizens. I attended the PUDR’s Saturday meetings at the Triveni Kala Sangam, paid a very modest amount from my stipend to help fund its reports, and on one occasion even joined a fact-finding group it had organised.

I was never a core member of PUDR, merely a fellow traveller, a sympathiser hovering around its outer circle. However, I admired the organisation and its work enormously, and thus felt a certain kinship with it, which was lost when I left Delhi for Bangalore in the early 1990s. Memories of what the PUDR had once meant to me came back while reading Ankita Pandey’s recently published book, Becoming Allies: Civil Liberties Activism in India .

Pandey views civil liberties groups as an illustration of what she calls “ally activism”, defined as “collective action undertaken in solidarity with a marginalized group by those who do not have a direct, personal or material stake in the cause”. As she observes, there have been two broad trends in the civil liberties movement in India; one that focuses on safeguarding the rights of citizens as codified in the Constitution, a second that canvasses for broader social and economic rights.

By all accounts, the oldest civil liberties group in independent India is the Calcutta-based Association for Protection of Democratic Rights, which took shape in the early 1970s. Among its early campaigns was to urge the humane treatment in prison of those associated with the Naxalite movement. The prisoners themselves had launched a bidi-chiththi andolan , demanding access to cigarettes and letters from friends and family. The APDR then amplified these demands to include better food and living conditions, and also the release of the prisoners themselves.

If the APDR was chronologically the first of these groups, then perhaps the most wide-ranging in its work has been the PUDR. Over the decades, the PUDR has published close to three hundred reports, documenting such issues as police brutality against undertrials, encounter deaths, the precarious condition of unorganised labour, laws dispossessing tribals of rights to forests and other natural resources, crimes against women, violence against Dalits, and State discrimination against religious minorities. Many (though not all) of these reports are available on the PUDR website.

Other important human rights groups in India include the People’s Union for Civil Liberties, headquartered in Delhi but with branches in several states, and whose prime mover was the jurist, V.M. Tarkunde; the Andhra Pradesh Civil Liberties Committee; the Human Rights Forum, also active in Andhra Pradesh; and the Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, which operates largely in Maharashtra, and one of whose founders was the social activist, Asghar Ali Engineer.

A key chapter in Pandey’s book focuses on the fact-finding reports that are “the predominant mode of activism for civil liberties groups in India”. These reports seek to document the culpability of the State and State officials in fuelling violence and thereby violating the safety, security, and democratic rights of citizens. They are based on the findings of individuals deputed to conduct an on-the-spot investigation of the events concerned.

Pandey argues that these fact-finding reports have served three key functions. First, they “transformed people’s recollections into legally helpful artefacts. The teams systematised, verified and documented testimonies in a form that would render them acceptable to a judicial commission or a court”. Second, these reports contained “a detailed description of the context and history to counter the technical and depersonalised official records of the same events”. And “the third element in the practice of fact-finding was locating gaps, outlining inconsistencies and exposing fudged records within the police and administrative documentation and reports.”

In sum, these fact-finding reports have aimed “to contradict, expose and highlight the inconsistencies in the official narratives in order to question their credibility in the eyes of the press and the public. They brought governmental wrongdoing to the spotlight and exposed the biases and prejudices of state functionaries”.

These civil liberties groups are entirely volunteer-driven, sustained by the work of individuals committed to their cause. They do not take foreign or corporate funds and tirelessly labour on in the face of societal prejudice and State hostility. Apart from the external pressures on their functioning, they also face an internal challenge; namely, to demonstrate that, while being critical of the State, they are at the same time independent of all political parties.

A second internal challenge these groups have had to confront is the question of gender justice. Some of the leading activists of groups like PUDR and the APCLC were women. However, their male colleagues thought the focus should be exclusively on the public violence committed by the State against citizens, arguing that violence within the domain of the family or the household should not be their concern. This was questioned by the female activists, who pointed out, for example, that in several parts of India the number of dowry deaths exceeded the number of custodial deaths. Eventually, these groups came to acknowledge that women’s rights were indeed a key part of a broader framework of democratic rights and incorporated this element in their work.

In Becoming Allies , Ankita Pandey notes that those active in civil liberties groups are disproportionately drawn from three professions; academics, journalism, and the law. These members of the salaried middle-class are animated by a spirit of sacrifice and idealism, seeking to make India a more just and humane society. Their character is often marked by self-effacement, downplaying their own role. Pandey quotes the activist lawyer, Sudha Bharadwaj, the daughter of two eminent academics and herself a graduate of the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology at Kanpur, as saying about her incarceration by the Indian State: “No doubt three years in jail has been painful, but there are many people more unfortunate than me. My heart went out to them. When you are in the midst of so much misery, it is difficult to be miserable for oneself; you have to help others.”

This self-effacement was also characteristic of the late C.V. Subba Rao, for many years the moving spirit of the PUDR. He goes unmentioned in Becoming Allies , even though the book starts with Who are the Guilty , the landmark report on the anti-Sikh riots of 1984. Subba Rao played a key role in the writing of this report, as in giving shape to the work of the PUDR more broadly. His absence from Pandey’s narrative is not be held against her, for it is merely a mark of how the man himself refused ever to take any credit for the work he did for others. One had to meet and observe Subba Rao in flesh and blood to know him for what he really was, namely, a true hero of Indian democracy.

Such omissions notwithstanding, Ankita Pandey’s Becoming Allies provides a valuable overview of the civil liberties movement as a whole and may be read in conjunction with the late Nilanjan Dutta’s Civil Liberties Movement in India: From Colonial Times to the Present . These books are particularly timely in the present context, when democratically-minded citizens face multiple threats — from, among other things, the apathy of the media, the brutality of the police, the indifference of the courts, and the active opposition of the Narendra Modi regime. In light of a creeping authoritarianism and a galloping majoritarianism, India now needs civil liberties activists more than ever.

editorials.title: Beyond map battles
editorials.passage:
China’s recurrent attempts to rename places in Arunachal Pradesh prompted India to identify and standardise the names of 27 places and geographical features in the state on official Survey of India maps. The Indian list includes strate­gically and historically significant locations like Longju, Maja, Bisa, Thag La, Dzo La, Riza La and Pukur La.

At first sight, this may appear to be merely a contest over place names. In reality, it is part of a much larger struggle involving history, administration, demography and territorial sovereignty. China’s actions appear designed to take advantage of ambiguities in the Agreement between the Government of the Republic of India and the Government of the Peoples Republic of China on the Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for the Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question. Signed in New Delhi on April 11, 2005, the agreement was intended to establish the broad political principles for resolving the boundary dispute. It did not demarcate the border or recognise either country’s territorial claims. Instead, it envisaged a three-stage process: agreement on political principles, negotiation of a framework for settlement, and eventual delineation and demarcation of the boundary.

The agreement affirmed that the dispute should be settled peacefully. It called upon both sides to make “meaningful and mutually acceptable adjustments” and arrive at a comprehensive package settlement covering the entire India-China boundary.

Two provisions have now acquired particular importance. Article V requires the two countries to take into account historical evidence, national sentiments, practical difficulties, reasonable concerns and sensitivities, and the actual state of the border areas. Article VII provides that the “due interests” of settled populations in border areas should be safeguarded.

When the agreement was concluded, Article VII was widely considered advantageous to India. Arunachal Pradesh, particularly Tawang, has a longstanding population living under Indian administration. Its residents are Indian citizens, participate in parliamentary and assembly elections and are governed by Indian constitutional, judicial and administrative institutions. Transferring such a populated area to China would gravely disturb the lives, rights and political identity of its inhabitants.

The wording of Article VII, however, is not entirely unambiguous. It does not explicitly prohibit the transfer of populated territory. It merely requires that the “due interests” of settled populations be protected. China could argue that such interests might be safeguarded even under a change of sovereignty. India’s more persuasive interpretation is that protecting these populations necessarily means not transferring them against their wishes.

China appears to be developing a strategy that combines renaming, settlement construction and administrative incorporation. It periodically publishes Chinese, Tibetan and Roman-script names for places in Arunachal Pradesh, which it calls Zangnan or South Tibet. By incorporating these names into official maps, gazetteers, digital databases and government records, Beijing seeks to create a documentary trail suggesting a historical and administrative relationship between these places and Tibet.

China has also constructed hundreds of xiaokang , or moderately prosperous villages in Tibet’s border regions. Many are located on the Chinese side of the Line of Actual Control, although some reportedly lie in disputed areas. These villages are equipped with roads, telecommunications, public buildings and other infrastructure that may serve civilian as well as military purposes.

Over time, China could invoke these settlements as evidence of effective administration and a permanent civilian presence. It might then rely upon Article V’s reference to the “actual state of border areas” and Article VII’s protection of “settled populations” to strengthen its territorial claims.

Such an interpretation must be firmly contested. A distinction should be drawn between historically-rooted indigenous communities and settlements created or expanded by the State for strategic purposes. Populations deliberately moved into disputed areas after the 2005 agreement cannot reasonably be given the same historical or moral weight as communities that have inhabited Arunachal Pradesh for generations.

India’s identification of 27 places is, therefore, a legitimate and useful response. It removes cartographic ambiguity, preserves India’s historical terminology and challenges China’s attempt to monopolise the naming narrative. But its effectiveness should not be exaggerated. Maps and names can support a territorial claim; they cannot by themselves create sovereignty.

India’s strongest case rests on its continuous and effective administration of Arunachal Pradesh, its democratic institutions, the participation of its people in India’s political life, and the population’s evident identification with India. The naming exercise must consequently be supplemented by stronger civil administration, infrastructure, telecommunications, livelihood opportunities and preservation of indigenous names and cultural traditions in frontier areas.

At the same time, India and China must prevent the battle of maps from foreclosing diplomacy. The first requirement is to stabilise the LAC. The two sides should exchange maps showing their respective perceptions, regulate patrolling in overlapping claim areas, establish joint verification procedures and prohibit new settlements or permanent military structures in mutually identified disputed pockets.

They should also agree upon a cut-off date — preferably April 11, 2005 —for determining which populations qualify as historically-settled communities under Article VII. Customary grazing grounds, pilgrimage routes, monasteries, sacred sites and indigenous patterns of land use should be jointly documented.

The ultimate settlement will require realism on both sides. The most practicable package would broadly convert the existing pattern of territorial control into an internationally recognised boundary: China accepting Indian sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh, including Tawang, and India accepting Chinese control over most of Aksai Chin, subject to limited and reciprocal adjustments.

Tawang’s religious and cultural links with Tibetan Buddhism can be protected without compromising Indian sovereignty. India could guarantee regulated pilgrimage, monastic exchanges, heritage conservation and scholarly interaction. Cultural association must not automatically be converted into territorial ownership.

Most importantly, the people of Arunachal Pradesh must be consulted. Their future cannot be negotiated exclusively by officials in New Delhi and Beijing. A settlement that disregards their wishes would violate the democratic spirit underlying the protection of settled populations.

India and China cannot redraw history, but they can prevent competing versions of history from determining their future. A realistic boundary settlement would remove a dangerous source of military confrontation, release resources for development, and enable two great Asian countries to pursue cooperation without recurring Himalayan crises. Names have symbolic power, but peace will ultimately require agreement on territory, security and, above all, the rights of the people who live there.

D. Jeevan Kumar is a Professor of Political Science at St. Claret College (Autonomous), Ziro, Arunachal Pradesh. Views are personal

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Setting the dinner menu is the prerogative of the host government
editorials.passage:
Sir — The vice-president of the United States of America, J.D. Vance, recently claimed that the OTT show, Emily in Paris, is the modern-day equivalent of Shakespearean writing. That is high praise from a Republican leader for a show about a young woman focusing on her career rather than building a life around a man. The irony of such a statement from Vance who belongs to a party known to term single and childless women as ‘crazy cat ladies’ is not lost on anyone. Here is a politician praising a fictional woman’s independence while working hard to take it away from real women.

Sir — The article, “When millet trumped meat” (Sept 17), raised an interesting question about hospitality, cultural sensitivity and food choices at international gatherings. The menu served to visiting dignitaries at the BRICS Summit was vegetarian. India undoubtedly has a rich and diverse vegetarian culinary tradition and presenting this to international guests can be an excellent way of showcasing our food heritage. At the same time, India is also a predominantly non-vegetarian country and dietary preferences vary across regions and communities. A thoughtful menu could showcase India’s traditional vegetarian delicacies alongside suitable non-vegetarian options. Celebrating our culinary heritage need not come at the cost of diversity.

Shibaji Roy Choudhuri, Calcutta

Sir — Serving an entirely vegetarian menu to foreign dignitaries from countries that relish meat is less hospitality and more culinary imposition dressed up as tradition. India’s strength lies in its extraordinary variety and diversity. Yet, somewhere along the way, ideology has quietly overtaken everything else. Jawhar Sircar rightly notes the irony of such a menu since most of India remains non-vegetarian, making the BRICS menu less reflective of the nation and more of those in power.

K. Chidanand Kumar, Bengaluru

Sir — Jawhar Sircar bases his arguments against serving only vegetarian dishes to foreign dignitaries at the BRICS Summit on the conjecture that they were deeply disappointed to find no non-vegetarian dish at the diplomatic dinner. He overlooks the fact that setting the dinner menu is the prerogative of the host government. Serving a strictly vegetarian menu at events does not amount to imposing dietary preferences on others. Delegates can eat what they prefer at their hotels. With the world’s largest vegetarian population and a rich tradition of vegetarian cuisine, showcasing a menu to reflect the same to guests is not inappropriate.

Sir — Language, culture and religion are among the things that define a group’s identity and any attempt to suppress these can often spark violence (“Weak link”, Sept 17). While celebrating Hindi Diwas is fine, promoting Hindi as the ‘national language’ ignores India’s constitutional commitment to diversity. The three-language policy is designed to protect this variety, at least on paper. It should not become a way to impose Hindi on the southern states.

A.G. Rajmohan, Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh

Sir — Referring to Hindi as a ‘link’ language rather than a competitor to regional languages, as the Union home minister done, highlights the Central government’s covert motive to replace English with Hindi. In India, English has been the ‘link’ language for years. But recent government circulars have adopted a dual Hindi and English approach, which remains unacceptable to many regions. The Central Board of Secondary Education categorising English as a ‘foreign’ language further cements the Centre’s intention of disregarding it.

Abhijit Chakraborty, Howrah

editorials.title: Tradition’s hammer: Editorial on the cost of curbing Durga Puja creativity
editorials.passage:
Strictures diminish creativity. The outburst of creativity in themes, images and pandals in Durga Puja seems to have received a check with the change in government in West Bengal. There are whispers that diktats have been issued regarding the height of the images and the shape of the goddess’s face: these have been fixed. There must be no aesthetic experimentation: the deity’s face must be rounded and her 10 arms all in one place. An old circular did limit the height of the images to 11 feet, but organisers and artists took some liberties. Now it is the rule. The chief minister has said that the images, pandals and themes should not be such that they hurt the religious and cultural tradition of Durga Puja. Clearly the new government and its sibling, the Vishwa Hindu Parishad — it was the first to lay down strictures — are among the elect since they not only know how the goddess should be worshipped but also how tall she is and what she looks like. Most important, they know that the way the goddess has been worshipped in Bengal all these years, with joy, reverence and rituals enveloped in warmth, beauty, variety and inclusiveness, has to be corrected. Thus the new stipulations regarding how the Pujas ought to be conducted.

It is not surprising that the mood in Kumartuli, the hub for image-creation, is muted. Most makers are playing it ‘safe’. Besides, their earnings have been badly hit this time. The number of orders has dropped. Not all organisers have claimed the one lakh-rupee grant given by the government and some of the bigger Puja committees feel that they do not have sufficient funds. On top of that, only 10 or 12 theme idols have been ordered in place of around 150 last year. The makers now have to rein in their artistic skills and play according to given rules, while suffering from growing economic insecurity even during the most lucrative season for them. The cost of raw materials has risen too, and the special clay needed for the idols has become scarce. Pandal -makers and light designers may have their creativity stifled too. No one can be quite sure as to what would constitute an offence to tradition. So, for these artists too, earnings in the most prosperous period of the year would fall.

The loss of creative magnificence would be a major factor in diminishing the excitement of the Pujas. This would have other ramifications. Over the years, in a state starved of business and investments, the economic turnover of the Durga Puja has been impressive consistently. The creative dimension of the Pujas, research has pointed out, played a significant role in augmenting its economic returns. But now, the endeavour to separate rituals from the idea of a festival — Durga Puja cannot be festive; it is not an utsav — has landed a blow to the Pujas’ inherent innovative essence. The consequences will not merely be aesthetic but also economic.

editorials.title: Lessons from TN rice price spike
editorials.passage:
The price of rice, Tamil Nadu’s staple food, has risen sharply over the past few weeks. The prices of certain varieties of rice have surged by more than ₹15-₹30 per kg, severely impacting household budgets.

While immediate blame is placed on rainfall deficits caused by El Nino and the subsequent drought in the Cauvery delta districts, the primary drivers of this price hike are — policy apathy, decades of structural neglect, and persistent production deficits in Tamil Nadu’s agricultural sector.

Researchers had long predicted the rise in prices of Tamil Nadu’s agricultural commodities due to shrinking cultivated area and a stagnant growth in irrigated area. However, the surge in rice prices has unfolded far more rapidly than anticipated. For over 30 years, Tamil Nadu has failed to achieve significant progress in cultivation technology or production growth not only in paddy but across other major crops.

Due to land-use changes triggered by urban agglomeration, Tamil Nadu’s Gross Cropped Area (GCA) continues to shrink, while paddy area has plummeted drastically. At a time when the total cropped area and paddy area are expanding at the national level, Tamil Nadu’s paddy area has shrunk from around 27 lakh hectares (lha) in 1970-71 to 19 lha in 2024-25.

As a result, Tamil Nadu is forced to rely heavily on Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka to meet its rice demand, particularly for fine varieties.

Tamil Nadu’s share in India’s total paddy production has also steadily declined over time.

A leading paddy-producing State in the 1970s, Tamil Nadu’s national contribution has now shrivelled to around 5 per cent.

States like Punjab and Haryana prioritised agricultural development by introducing improved irrigation facilities, modern mechanisation and high-yielding seed varieties, which pushed their yields above 4,400 kg per hectare in 2024-25.

In contrast, Tamil Nadu’s average paddy yield has remained stagnant at 3,200-3,300 kg per hectare for years now. Due to the low yields, farmers have largely abandoned the cultivation of fine rice varieties like Ponni.

Farmers are turning away from paddy cultivation because the returns fail to cover even the cost of cultivation. Data released by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) show that the cost of cultivation of paddy in Tamil Nadu is high at ₹99,902/ha in 2024-25.

In contrast, the major paddy-producing States like Odisha, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal incur costs ranging only between ₹83,563 and ₹87,806/ha.

As a result, farmers find cultivation unprofitable. Based on the comprehensive cost of cultivation (C2 cost) data from 1974-75 to 2021-22, paddy farmers in Tamil Nadu made a profit in only 15 of those years. Since 2000-01, they have turned a profit in just three years, while paddy farmers in Punjab earned a profit in every single year except for one.

Increased farm wages, machinery rentals, irrigation costs and fertilizer and pesticide prices have steeply driven up cultivation costs of crops in Tamil Nadu. The Minimum Support Price (MSP) fixed by the Central and State governments (including state bonuses) has not risen to cover this escalation in production costs. Consequently, paddy farmers are trapped in a cycle of debt and economic distress.

This stagnation is not confined to rice alone. Comparing three-year average crop production data, taking 1980-1983 and 2019-2022, shows that Tamil Nadu’s contribution to India’s total output has dropped significantly for almost all major crops, except maize (see Table).

Paddy’s contribution fell from 8.62 per cent to 5.64 per cent, red gram (tur) dropped from 2.13 per cent to 1.19 per cent, total oilseeds plunged from 9.31 per cent to 3.01 per cent, groundnut declined from 15.82 per cent to 10.23 per cent, cotton shrivelled from 3.20 per cent to 0.94 per cent, and sugarcane dropped from 10.18 per cent to 3.59 per cent during this period. El Nino cannot entirely be blamed. Prices of other agricultural commodities like pulses, oilseeds, cotton, sugar and vegetables could also rise sharply in the future.

The neglect of agriculture has resulted in shrinking of irrigated areas, increase in fallow land and reduction in cultivated areas in Tamil Nadu, leading to price spikes. Tamil Nadu’s inflation rate in May 2026 reached 5.11 per cent, against the national average of 3.93 per cent. Crop prices cannot be controlled without boosting domestic agricultural production. Therefore, the Tamil Nadu government must formulate policies to increase crop output.

First, the government should immediately constitute a committee consisting of top agricultural experts to formulate short- and long-term plans to accelerate agricultural growth in the State. Second, to incentivise farmers, the Tamil Nadu government should provide State incentives based on realistic production cost data published by CACP to fix a fair procurement price for paddy and other crops.

Third, the State must increase the number of Direct Procurement Centres (DPCs) to ensure swift procurement of paddy without middleman interference, and expand the number of warehouses and their storage capacity.

Fourth, following other States, crops should be procured directly by the State using Market Intervention Scheme by allocating adequate funds whenever prices crash.

Fifth, assured irrigation is paramount for agricultural growth so the State’s 40,000-plus tanks and all canals need to be restored to expand irrigation coverage. Sixth, micro-irrigation methods like drip and sprinkler should be actively promoted to ensure efficient water use.

To conclude, Tamil Nadu’s experience serves as a stark lesson for States that ignore agriculture. Policymakers must recognise that the current rise in rice prices in Tamil Nadu is not merely a temporary market aberration but an outcome of years of agricultural policy neglect. Unless the government takes measures to boost production, strengthen irrigation coverage and assure farmers’ income, farm prices will skyrocket impacting the consumers.

The writer is an economist and former full-time Member (Official), CACP, New Delhi. Views expressed are personal

editorials.title: UPI fees: The economics of ‘free’ payments
editorials.passage:
The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026 changed Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, giving the Centre power to specify which payment modes remain protected.

A September 14 gazette notification, followed by a September 15 NPCI circular, now protects UPI payments up to ₹2,000, while effective from October 15, a 0.4 per cent MDR will apply to person-to-merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000, with a ₹300 cap for payments above ₹75,000.

Person-to-merchant transactions in select sectors attract a lower rate or a flat fee, while person-to-person transfers remain free. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh a month through UPI QR codes are also exempt.

The introduction of Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on the erstwhile free popular mode of non-cash transaction has stirred quite a debate. Who should pay for a system that users so far regarded as free, and what would be the pros and cons?

UPI moves money instantly between bank accounts through an account-linked ID or a QR code. Beginning in 2016, it grew rapidly after demonetisation. In August 2026, UPI processed about 24.5 billion transactions worth nearly ₹30 trillion. Incentives like the zero-MDR drove that growth. The government also supported low-value transactions by approving subsidies to payment processors, which stood at ₹1,500 crore for payments of up to ₹2,000 to small merchants for 2024-25. The ease of transaction and instantaneous settlement were clear advantages over NEFT, which settles in one hour and requires sharing of account number and IFSC. Hence, UPI could compete with cash, so far.

UPI feels free because the payment processors bear its costs. Transaction processing and settlement, server maintenance, complaints handling, and fraud monitoring are as costly as ₹20,700 crore annually, according to the Parliamentary Standing Committee. Government support covers a minuscule share. That arrangement was easier when rapid adoption was the priority. But UPI is now a mature network. It needs continued spending to ensure security, reliability and capacity.

A 0.4 per cent MDR is a middle path. The fee gives banks and payment firms income to offset costs and invest in upgrades. Since it applies to person-to-merchant transactions above ₹2,000, only about 4 per cent by volume, but roughly two-thirds by value, everyday payments remain protected. However, fees on those high-value transactions are not trivial for businesses with thin margins. A merchant charged an MDR may not bear all of it. It can absorb the fee, raise prices or transfer it back onto customers as a service fee. How much is passed to customers will depend on competition and margins.

Will it push people away from UPI? Probably not by much. UPI is quick and familiar. Yet some larger purchases may shift to cash or bank transfers if merchants transfer the UPI fees. Credit Cards are not competitive since the present value of a typical 1.6 per cent transaction fee discounted over an average 30-day credit period at a 6 per cent cost-of-capital rate is approximately 1.1 per cent.

However, with NEFT mandated to be free by RBI, some of the high-value transactions may shift to NEFT. Some high-value transactions might also be split into batches of transactions below ₹2,000, unnecessarily burdening the system by increasing transaction traffic. With same-day clearing, the cheques may regain some relevance. Will these be regressive? Only time will tell.

More important implications lie elsewhere. UPI has moved transactions from cash into the digital system. Digital footprints can help lenders assess cash flows for credit scores, make economic activities easier to trace for tax purposes, detect fraud, and even solve crimes. When transactions move back to cash, those footprints vanish.

The government has tried to retain public benefit by supporting small merchants and low-value payments, while taxing higher ones. Neither the government nor banks need to bear the entire cost of a mature system. Larger merchants can contribute. A mixed funding model is fairer and more sustainable.

Masanpally is Assistant Professor of Strategy; Kundu is Assistant Professor of Finance at IMI Kolkata. Views expressed are personal

editorials.title: Poor in economic security
editorials.passage: India’s decline in poverty over the past decade is a major development achievement. Between 2011-12 and 2023-24, real GDP grew at about 6% a year, while the share of Indians living below the World Bank’s extreme-poverty line of $3 per person per day, measured in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) terms, fell from 27.1% to 2.6%. Growth accompanied by falling poverty is, in many ways, what development is supposed to look like. People also experience economic progress through what their work earns them. For most, work is the foundation on which economic security is built. A household may sustain consumption through the combined earnings of several members, government transfers, savings, borrowing, or informal support. These can all improve living standards, and their role matters. Earnings from work answer a different and more basic question. Is the economic value of a person's labour rising? ALSO READBoard audits: Myth, miracle, or mirage On that measure, India’s recent record is less straightforward. Between 2018 and 2025, India’s output per worker increased by about 2.3% a year in constant 2021 PPP terms, while real GDP expanded by roughly 5.21% annually. Roughly, these figures broadly imply employment growth of close to 2.9% a year. The economy therefore grew by employing more people as well as by producing more per worker. Yet among workers reporting positive labour income, median real earnings increased by only 1.47% CAGR, as seen through India’s labour data set, the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). The earnings of the typical worker grew more slowly than both the economy and output per worker. Aggregate growth is experienced in ordinary life through the income people can take home, what they can spend today, what they can save for tomorrow, and how much room they have to deal with an illness, a job loss, or an unexpected expense. A growing economy can create more jobs and produce more output while the purchasing power generated by ordinary work fails to keep pace. PLFS also shows that in constant 2021 PPP terms, the median worker earned about $16.76 a day in 2025, compared with $15.13 in 2017-18. In rural India, median earnings rose from $12.80 to $14.45 a day; in urban India, from $20.26 to $22.49. The urban median remained around 56% higher than the rural median in 2025, only slightly narrower than the 58% gap eight years earlier. The median, however, tells us only what happened to the worker in the middle. It does not tell us whether those at the bottom gained or whether their earnings were sufficient to cross even modest standards of purchasing power. ALSO READCrunch time This is where international poverty lines can be useful in a different way. The World Bank’s $3 and $4.20 lines are designed to measure household consumption poverty, not individual labour earnings. Applying them to PLFS earnings therefore does not produce another estimate of poverty. But they can serve as benchmarks of income adequacy: a way of asking how many workers earn less than the purchasing-power equivalent of standards associated with extreme poverty and different levels of country income. In that sense, they put an otherwise abstract earnings distribution on a more human scale. The bottom of the distribution tells a different story. Among rural workers reporting positive labour income, the share earning less than the equivalent of $3 a day rose from 3.83% in 2017-18 to 4.63% in 2025. In urban India, it increased only marginally, from 1.48% to 1.56%. By 2025, the incidence was therefore almost three times as high among rural workers as among urban workers. At the $4.20-a-day benchmark, the international poverty standard associated with lower-middle-income countries, which India is, the unevenness is sharper. Nationally, the share of workers earning below the benchmark increased from 5.62% to 6.83%. In rural India, it rose from 6.58% to 8.62%. In urban India, it declined from 3.53% to 2.33%. The significance of this rural deterioration is difficult to dismiss as a small corner of the labour market. Nearly 68% of India’s workforce was rural in 2025. For a very large majority of workers, therefore, economic progress is still being experienced through a labour market in which earnings remain considerably lower than in urban India and where the poorest-paid workers have seen little improvement. This contextualises India’s progress in reducing consumption poverty measures. Consumption and labour income measure different things. A household generally pools resources. It might receive subsidised food or other transfers that protect basic consumption, and savings or borrowing can smooth difficult periods. As a result, poverty can fall even when the earnings remain weak. That said, even the poverty story is not so simple. India has not simply crossed one poverty threshold and finished the development journey. In 2023-24, 16.1% of the population, around 232 million people, still lived below the World Bank’s $4.20-a-day lower-middle-income-country poverty line. Rural poverty at this benchmark was 19.34%, compared with 8.6% in urban India. So, while India has made extraordinary progress in moving people away from extreme deprivation, crossing a minimum threshold is not the same as building economic security. For that, people also need work where purchasing power rises steadily over time. This is why labour income deserves a place alongside GDP growth and poverty reduction when we think about development. Poverty tells us whether people have crossed a minimum. In contrast, labour earnings tell us whether work is carrying them further above it. India’s poverty reduction is real and worth celebrating. The next challenge is ensuring that ordinary work itself becomes steadily more rewarding, especially for the rural workers who still make up most of the country’s workforce. Development is not only about how much an economy produces, or even how much households consume. It is also about whether work leaves people meaningfully better off over time. Co-authored with Mukul Anand, researcher, Institute for Competitiveness Disclaimer: The views expressed are the author’s own and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express.

editorials.title: Board audits: Myth, miracle, or mirage
editorials.passage: Sebi requires listed entities to undertake annual performance evaluation of their boards, committees, and individual directors. Do the questionnaires, interviews, peer assessments, board observations, committee reviews, and external assessors actually make boards better? Recent India Inc upheavals have challenged the assumption that institutionally-owned entities necessarily have more effective boards than promoter-led entities. What did those effectiveness reviews reveal before the crises? Proper board effectiveness assessments go beyond scores to identify the conversation being avoided, the capability that is missing, the power dynamic distorting discussion, or the director whose contribution no longer matches organisational needs. A serious review should test four Cs: competency, capability, crisis management, and compliance. ALSO READIndia’s GDP roller coaster Often, annual board assessments can create a comforting belief that all is well, with directors quick to defend the expertise and experience they bring to the table. But individual accomplishment does not make a director effective. The four Cs must be judged in the context of the company. An annual evaluation and board-effectiveness audit are different. A deeper audit tests the four Cs against board papers, interviews, meeting observations, and consequential decisions to establish whether the board actually exercises judgement, challenge, and oversight. In India Inc, independent directors may have advisory or mentorship links to promoters, key shareholders, or the company. A relationship may satisfy the regulatory test for independence yet raise a deeper question: Does the proximity compromise independent judgement? Independent directors are also expected to protect minority shareholders. Can a board-effectiveness study reveal what the regulatory test cannot? When a professional services firm already advising the company arrives with a Western governance scorecard to assess its board, one may reasonably ask whether the mirror is truly independent. The same firm may have recruited the chairman, CEO, or an influential board member and later be asked to assess the board. Promoters and influential board members can be drawn to an exalted global name for the legitimacy it lends, but the imprimatur should never become a substitute for scrutiny. There is another organisational misjudgement. In some companies, the chairman’s executive assistant commissions the confidential board assessment and shortlists the assessor. Elsewhere, it sits within the C-suite or even the procurement head. These may appear organisationally convenient, but blur a governance boundary: this is the board’s work. The chairman or the nomination and remuneration committee (NRC) chairperson must run the process instead. ALSO READGeneva talks hold out promise Much of today’s boardroom is built on “reputation shopping”: Institutions borrow accomplished individuals’ credibility, while some directors encash reputations built elsewhere or past favours. But fear of being sidelined, displeasure, or even vendetta can make challenges costly. Board chemistry matters because judgement is shaped by differences in values, expertise, industry exposure, personalities, and stakeholder proximity. A deep assessment should thus test how the board exercises collective judgement over organisational strategy and culture, risk, and emerging vulnerabilities, while management remains accountable for execution. A board becomes a team only when directors trust and respect each other enough for candour, knowing that difficult truths can carry a social cost and sometimes strain the very relationships that make the board work. That is where an external assessor earns a real role — probing contradictions, observing meetings, and stress-testing if the board is active to its core purpose. Directors who ask difficult questions and hold their ground when the room would rather move on remain a minority. Too often, everyone is comfortable with the equilibrium until a crisis exposes what the board chose not to confront. The challenge is greater when the promoter is also the chairperson or the CEO has a larger-than-life reputation, and effectiveness exercises is perfunctory since the power equation is obvious. Collective findings are easy to accept. It becomes harder when the finding has a name. What if a director doesn’t understand the business, rarely prepares, dominates discussion, or contributes little? What if someone is strong on compliance but weak on strategy, or stale for the company’s new phase? Can the evaluation say it plainly, and will anyone act? Every material finding needs an owner, an action, and a review point. If the problem is board capability, develop it. If it is role-fit, change the role. If it can’t be remedied, have the succession conversation. Outlier chairpersons use these exercises differently. They want the mirror held close, even when it reflects badly on them, and ask the assessor to speak plainly. That is where the exercise earns its place. The evaluation test is of future-readiness: Does the board have the competence to understand changes, the capability to respond, the capacity to manage a crisis, and the judgement to distinguish compliance from a strategic or cultural warning? In some organisations, there are effectively two reports — the formal governance record and more informal observations shared only with a chairman or NRC chairperson who wants to understand what is happening, even if unable to act on every finding. The second conversation may contain the real governance value. That is why board-effectiveness audits can be myth, miracle, or mirage — myth when the exercise is mistaken for effectiveness, miracle when a board sees itself honestly and changes, and mirage when methodology creates comfort without altering the boardroom. In an era of investor activism, a board’s effectiveness and visible behavioural credibility matter equally. The real test is whether directors accept uncomfortable findings and “unlearn and learn” to become more effective members. Else, the board should save itself the rigmarole, the consultants’ fees, and the polished report. It has already decided there are truths it would rather not govern.
