editorials.title: Crunch time
editorials.passage: Even ahead of the 25-basis-point (bps) rate hike by the Federal Open Market Committee on Wednesday, rising and increasingly broad-based inflation at home, amid fairly strong growth momentum, provided sufficient reason for monetary policy to be tightened. Retail inflation in August hit 4.8% year-on-year, a far cry from the benign sub-3% levels at the start of the year. That is still well within the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) comfort zone, but there are signs that prices in some pockets are rising faster than before. Services are one such area, with relative softness giving way to firmer price pressures. What could really throw inflation off-kilter is the renewed surge in crude oil prices to over $100 a barrel, which has pushed the Indian crude basket to around $120-125 a barrel. With the crisis in West Asia worsening and Lindsey Graham’s Russia and Iran sanctions bill close to becoming a reality, India finds itself in a predicament. Supplies may or may not be severely disrupted, but the oil import bill can only get bigger, potentially compelling the government to resort to another round of petrol and diesel price increases. A hike of Rs 7.50 a litre, similar to the last round, could push inflation above 6%, making the central bank’s task considerably harder. ALSO READA nation learns by building Pressure points are also emerging in the food basket as vegetables, cereals, and sugar become costlier; food inflation is nudging 6% even before the effects of a less-than-normal monsoon and El Niño have been fully felt. If headline consumer price index inflation (CPI) has not yet moved above 5% or become “generalised”, it is partly because companies have yet to fully pass on higher input costs to consumers, as reflected in the gap between non-food wholesale price index and CPI inflation. That the pass-through is under way can be seen in the rise in super-core inflation, which excludes the impact of precious metals. Clearly, price pressures are becoming more broad-based, and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) needs to take this seriously, particularly before inflation expectations become entrenched. Even in the absence of a broad-based rise in prices, however, a recalibration of rates may be warranted. Core inflation is trending higher and should average a little over 4% this fiscal, while consensus estimates now peg headline inflation at 5.5-6% for the September-November period. Real interest rates, too, remain low. These factors have clearly not escaped the MPC’s attention. The minutes of the August meeting reflected a “hawkish hold”, somewhat at odds with the dovish tone of the policy statement and RBI commentary. Importantly, a recalibration need not be accompanied by a change in the policy stance — currently neutral — giving the RBI greater room for manoeuvre and allowing it to respond to incoming data. ALSO READGeneva talks hold out promise The rate-hiking cycle is likely to begin with a 25-bps increase in October, followed by a similar move in December, with the objective of anchoring inflation expectations. Much as in other countries, money is set to become costlier in India too. That is unfortunate because it would make loans more expensive for individuals and small businesses. A higher cost of capital at a time when growth is set to decelerate — to about 7% this year — cannot be helpful. One hopes the plentiful liquidity in the system will keep banks’ borrowing costs relatively low, allowing lending rates to remain reasonable. If the growth momentum is to be sustained, credit needs to remain affordable.

editorials.title: Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answer
editorials.passage:
F ar-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a little regional electoral victory for one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.

But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (Nazi Germany until 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.

Then there’s the fact that Germany is Europe’s central power. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel says that when her party gets into government after the federal election scheduled for 2029, Germany will abandon the euro and leave the Schengen border-free travel area. What would be left of the EU then?

The great German liberal social and political thinker Ralf Dahrendorf, who died in 2009 , told me more than once that he would only feel really confident of the resilience of German democracy when it had withstood the test of a big economic crisis. Well, the country is close to that now.

The final segment of “because it’s Germany!” is perhaps the most interesting. The federal republic’s entire constitutional, political and educational system is designed to prevent anything like the collapse of the Weimar republic into Hitler’s dictatorship in 1933. The federal republic should be a wehrhafte Demokratie – a democracy capable of defending itself.

So how Germany will defend its democracy is a question not just of European but of global significance. Looking at all the answers being frenetically canvassed in Berlin, I think the most convincing formula is: neither ban the AfD nor embrace it, but instead constrain it legally and fight it politically.

The German constitution provides for political parties that are “hostile” to its basic liberal democratic principles to be banned. Senior German politicians have called for an application to be made to the constitutional court to ban the AfD, or at least its most extreme parts, on those grounds. But it’s too late for that. The AfD has been a major force in the Bundestag since its success (off the back of the migration crisis) in the 2017 general election and, like Reform UK in Britain, has led nationwide in opinion polls. To suddenly tell so many citizens “you’re not allowed to vote for the party you support!” would itself be an assault on democracy.

But this is not democracy as the tyranny of the majority: the people have spoken, off with your head! It’s liberal democracy, meaning the outcome of any popular vote is constrained by the rule of law, human and minority rights, and pluralist, anti-majoritarian institutions. The real threats to German democracy today are less like Weimar in 1933 than Budapest in 2010 (when Viktor Orbán took over) and Washington DC in 2025. The mini-Donald Trumps of the AfD have reportedly been quietly exploring Trump-like executive and administrative devices they might use to consolidate their control . The Federal Republic of Germany has the right, the power and the duty to stop them.

Article 37 of the constitution, which allows federal authorities to overrule anti-constitutional behaviour by the states, has never been used in the 77-year history of the republic. Assuming, as now seems likely, the AfD forms the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, all federal powers, up to and including article 37, should be used wherever necessary. For example, they should prevent sensitive intelligence about Russia’s increasing aggression being shared with a Saxony-Anhalt branch of the domestic security service controlled by the pro-Russian AfD; secure the independence of courts and prosecutors, as well as the neutrality of police and civil service; and, I would add, stop any extreme politicisation of education and public service broadcasting. Of course, AfD politicians will cry “foul!”; tough. If, as they say, they want “another republic”, they can go and live in Russia.

Yet even more important than these legal and administrative constraints is the political response. At the opposite end from those calling for the party to be banned are Christian Democrats calling for the “firewall ” to be abandoned and AfD politicians to be embraced as part of the normal political process. Letting them take responsibility in a state government will, it’s argued, expose their incoherence, incompetence and lack of real policy answers.

Talking and working with them will end up moderating them, as apparently happened with Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. I’ve been tempted by these arguments myself. But evidence collected by political scientists suggests that a strategy of inclusion is just as likely to put more wind in the nationalists’ sails. And AfD activists are themselves warning against the danger of Melonisierung (Melonisation).

So Christian Democrats should not be tempted to get half into bed with the AfD, like a middle-aged man nervously edging into an extramarital affair. Instead, starting already this weekend with elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, they should more effectively combat it politically. Rather than defining Christian Democracy by what it’s against (the AfD and the far-left Linke), they should say what it’s for. To renew Germany’s social market economy, they should implement all the labour market, pension, tax and other reforms agreed this summer with their Social Democrat coalition partners – and more. Faced with huge external challenges, from Russian aggression to US and Chinese AI, the Christian Democrats – historically the party of Europe – should boldly advocate the European-scale answers which alone will give any European country the strength to stand up to giants.

But besides AI, Germany’s mainstream parties badly need EI (emotional intelligence). The key to the success of the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund in Saxony-Anhalt, as with Trump and Britain’s Nigel Farage, is a kind of emotional communication. I’m here with you; I hear you and see you; I share your anger. With me, you can say what you really think and be yourself, because – whether or not I’m a millionaire – deep down I’m a normal bloke like you. So let’s all have a beer and march forward to an imagined past.

It’s fascinating to re-read the exiled German political scientist Karl Loewenstein’s influential 1937 article on “militant democracy” and find him insisting that democracy cannot “devise emotional formulas capable of competing with the fascist Pied Pipers”. Hence the emphasis on constitutional constraints. But in our transformed information environment, with its premium on attention, drama and passion, democracy can’t be defended simply by legal constraints and rational policies. Democrats everywhere need to compete with today’s Pied Pipers on the emotional plane, too. Constant presence on social media and physical presence on the ground are both essential.

Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, and to some extent the UK’s, Andy Burnham, have shown how it can be done. So much will now depend on German democrats, and especially Christian Democrats, proving they can do the same.

Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters , is published in October

editorials.title: Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was
editorials.passage:
I t must have come as a surprise to Ed Sheeran when all of his support acts withdrew from the remainder of the US leg of his tour. The American rapper Macklemore had triggered the walkout when he gave an impassioned speech calling for a “free Palestine” on stage and was dropped for doing so. The decision by the remaining acts to drop out in solidarity exposed a deep divide in the modern music industry. Some artists still insist on keeping politics out of music, while others expect music to speak to our perilous times.

After he was dropped, Macklemore wrote that Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before”, to which Sheeran responded : “I am not complicit” and “those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum”.

I think that the concept of expectation is worth probing. The idea that artists should make their political sentiments known is often dismissed as a parasocial delusion, one particularly rampant among young people on social media who “call out” musicians for their silence (indeed, young people are far more likely to be in favour of musicians using their concerts to make political statements ). Artists aren’t politicians, the criticism goes, and to consider them as such distracts from, even compromises, the purpose of art as a forum for personal expression and of escapism. In other words, why not just enjoy the music instead of expecting activism from musicians, too?

The problem with that idea is that it treats a separation of art and politics as natural rather than something determined by historical convention. It wasn’t so long ago that expectations were quite different. There used to be a neater division between countercultural musicians who were relegated to the periphery and mainstream artists who would be disciplined if they spoke up.

The MTV era of music in the 2000s prioritised blockbuster, spectacle and glamour, while avoiding political, social and economic controversies. Artists were generally expected to keep politics out of their music. When Madonna challenged that idea in 2003 with her single American Life, which opposed US foreign policy and jingoism at the onset of the Iraq war, the backlash was heavy: she was forced to dump its “un-American” music video, and faced heavy radio blacklisting. It took years for the Chicks , then known as The Dixie Chicks, to recover commercially from the backlash they faced to their criticism of the Iraq War and George W Bush around the same period.

Today, the expectations that audiences have of artists are different from two decades ago. Partly, this is because the economics and the technology behind the music industry has changed. In the age of streaming, it is harder to silence artists who have made politically problematic statements – radio station blacklisting is far less fatal than it was before people discovered music through their phones and algorithms.

Interestingly, this greater political autonomy also means that the biggest artists take less of a commercial hit in their worst moments. After Kanye West’s antisemitic rants (which the rapper apologised for), his album Vultures still reached No 1 on the Billboard charts in 2024. On his most recent tour, he performed at AT&T stadium in Arlington, Texas, one of the venues that banned Macklemore from performing.

In any case, this greater autonomy pushes young fans to ask: why not take the risk? Why not speak? Particularly in the case of Palestine, it has often been smaller and less influential artists who have done so. Think of how the scale of Sheeran’s commercial reach, by contrast, dwarfs that of the artists around him who have risked more by speaking out.

Artists, both alternative and mainstream, have also set this expectation for each other. The stances a musician has taken on pressing issues are no longer just cudgels used against them. Rather, silence on these matters has become a source of shame.

Billie Eilish rebuked her fellow celebrities for not taking a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the US and its killing of civilians . The Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, who I saw at Glastonbury last year leading a “free Palestine” chant on the Pyramid Stage, had this to say while receiving the award for best album at the Ivor Novello Awards this year: “I have a very specific idea of what songwriting is supposed to be for, and I think it is to reflect the times through your own personal view so that everybody can have something to connect to and something to learn from years later. And now I would compel my fellow artists in the room, it is not the time to sit on the fence.”

The political shift in music also reflects a tonal shift. Artists have become more emotionally intimate with their audiences. I was struck by an analysis published earlier this year by the music data company Musixmatch for the Economist, which assessed lyrics from the Billboard charts to conclude that pop music has become “gloomier”. The most popular songs increasingly invoke sadness, angst and heartbreak.

A study in the Times also found that the musical mood has become more downbeat . This is in itself not surprising – listeners increasingly want authenticity from musicians and depend on it for a sense of connection. Think of the music of Eilish and CMAT, both of whom are popular with young audiences and praised for filterless emotion. They invoke that gloom, vulnerability and emotion – in other words, they communicate pain as a central tenor of their sound.

As CMAT said of her music, which muses on isolation, capitalism and disillusionment: “Everyone has the same wants and desires, and if you’re really honest as an artist with your pain, it will always connect.” For many young people, part of the pain they have felt in the past few years has been in witnessing the events in Gaza, as well as the rising global tide of far-right populism , the climate crisis and instability. So for a generation that is increasingly accustomed to having their despair made audible through gloomier music, why would they not increasingly expect artists to draw connections between their personal pain and what is causing it?

Artists, then, cannot assume that the old bargain still holds. Sheeran’s insistence on an apolitical arena of music is increasingly anachronistic – a position that has exposed the faultlines of modern music. Many listeners increasingly seek emotional clarity as well as moral clarity. Whether popular music has risen to that moment will be judged by history. But for now, as the expectation changes, it is down to artists to decide if they change with it.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

editorials.title: After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly
editorials.passage:
M ore than 20 years ago, when I started the campaign and TV series School Dinners , I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our children at school. I have never, and will never, stop banging that drum – even after this week’s momentous announcement on school food standards in England. Because it is so important we remember where we started from.

Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, but twice the recommended sugar , school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.

But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’s social connection and sense of belonging . Well-fed kids are happier , have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, and their learning and behaviour improve, too .

It’s no surprise that 80% of teachers agree that unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.

But we didn’t need scientific evidence to tell us that – who doesn’t feel and perform better when their bellies are full of the good stuff? Get school food right and the prize is massive. Not just for children today, but for the adults they will become. Feed children well and we give them a better chance of healthier lives, greater productivity and less long-term pressure on the NHS and social care from diet-related disease. That’s no small change when current estimates are that obesity, and its knock-on consequences, costs the UK economy about £126bn each year .

That is why it’s so great to see the government announce new standards, based on the latest science. It’s the first time in a decade. And it means, for this generation of kids, they will be nourished with more fruit and vegetables, fibre-rich proteins and whole grains. Beautiful stuff.

It’s a big and much-needed update, but we know that amazing schools, caterers and chefs can rise to the challenge. Through my Good School Food awards , we have shown amazing school food is possible and affordable, and it’s happening right now in schools across the UK.

Take Chef Russ in Bournemouth . Working out of a cupboard-sized kitchen, he has transformed the food at his school. Not only has the school increased the uptake of meals from 28% to 98%, there’s a waiting list of parents keen to nab their kids a place there.

We see this pattern in schools up and down the country, and we have to keep telling these stories again and again because it goes against what many people think they know – that kids simply won’t eat the “good stuff”. We have heard that for decades. And we get it, because the food environment we all struggle with makes it hard to eat well, and so this seems to chime with our experience. But school is different. It’s a rare, protected space where that noise can be stripped away.

And when it is, remarkable things happen. Children eat – and enjoy – delicious, nutritious food. The evidence is clear: when the food is good and the environment is supportive, over time school meal uptake increases.

What makes me excited is these standards won’t just sit on a piece of paper. There will be proper monitoring to make sure they are actually followed. Not to nit-pick. Not to catch schools out. But so we know what’s working, where schools are doing brilliantly, and where we need to deploy care, love and support to help them get it right. That’s where the School Food Project comes in. We know not all lunch trays are created equal, which is why we are partnering with Bite Back, Chefs in Schools, School Food Matters and the Food Foundation to help to make sure these new standards can really be for everyone.

These new school food standards will finally fix what is on children’s school plates, but it’s only half the job we have to do. A delicious lunch nourishes a child for the afternoon, but teaching them how to cook nourishes them for the rest of their life. You can serve the best meals in the world, but if a child leaves school without knowing how to feed themselves, that’s where it stops.

That is why food education must be absolutely central to transforming school food. And it’s why I’m passionate about giving kids (and adults) the skills, knowledge and confidence to cook from scratch. My dream has always been simple: I want every single child to leave school knowing 10 core skills that will save their life.

My free 10 skills food education programme teaches kids basic, bulletproof culinary foundations – how to chop safely, balance flavours, cook a nutritious staple meal from scratch, and stretch simple, fresh ingredients into something delicious. If kids leave school knowing how to cook a fast vegetable stir-fry, a simple soup, or how to make a loaf of bread, not only will they be healthier now, but they have options in the future.

With this cooking superpower they can feed themselves, and their future families, on a budget. That isn’t just a life skill: it’s health insurance for life.

Jamie Oliver is a chef, restaurateur and campaigner

editorials.title: Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles
editorials.passage:
Sometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.

For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.

Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours after US Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow .

Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time.

I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time.

editorials.title: Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
editorials.passage:
Russia’s parliamentary elections offer an excellent opportunity for a new round in the information war between the West and Russia. Western politicians, experts and journalists have been given yet another convenient occasion to tell their target audiences that democracy has long ceased to exist in Russia; that the federal parliament, like any other representative body, in practice determines nothing in Russian life; and that all genuinely important decisions for the country are made not even by the government but exclusively in the Kremlin, by an extremely narrow circle of individuals accountable to no one.

Therefore, in the view of many critics of the Russian authorities, elections in Russia need not have been held at all: their outcome was predetermined by Kremlin political strategists and, in any event, will have no significant impact on the country’s future.

And yet even the most biased outside observer could hardly fail to notice the obvious: the Russian authorities made consistent and persistent efforts to ensure that these elections attracted the highest possible participation and were conducted successfully under current electoral law. For at least the past several months, the country had experienced heightened political activity.

Leading politicians and state officials constantly reminded the electorate of the importance of the coming elections. Governors of politically “problematic” regions were urgently allocated additional subsidies. Payments to certain categories of public-sector employees and pensioners were hastily indexed. And inevitable but unpopular or painful decisions for the public – for example, the forthcoming significant nationwide increase in housing and utility tariffs – were postponed until after the elections.

Even possible shifts in Russia’s position on the conflict with Ukraine and future relations with the West were often linked in public and political discussions to the results of the September elections, which were supposedly meant to “untie the hands” of the Russian leadership, although there were very different, sometimes diametrically opposed, views about how exactly the leadership would use these “untied hands”. In any case, it must be acknowledged that the Kremlin did not take the easy path of its opponents in Kyiv, who simply postponed the 2024 Ukrainian presidential election until better, “postwar” times, despite clear discontent and muted grumbling from part of Ukraine’s political class.

What is going on here? Why should the Kremlin invest so much energy and so many resources in what is often interpreted outside Russia as little more than an unconvincing simulation of genuine political competition? Why launch a new full electoral cycle while a large-scale military conflict has yet to end, when the normal boundaries of peacetime political democracy tend, one way or another, to narrow?

It is difficult to suppose that holding elections in Russia is driven solely by Kremlin strategists’ obsessive desire to impress, at all costs, either their external opponents or their partners abroad. As for the former, they would not change their views about the nature of the Russian political system, even in the hypothetical event that the elections ended in a complete triumph for the radical opposition and a crushing defeat for all pro-Kremlin candidates. Such a scenario would most likely lead to endless speculation about yet another “cunning Putin plan”, intended to mislead a credulous Western public and conceal the consistently authoritarian nature of Russia’s political regime.

As for the latter, it is hard to imagine that the leaders of Iran, North Korea, Belarus or China are seriously concerned about the state or future of Russian democracy. The political systems of their countries, like those of many other foreign friends and partners of Russia, to put it mildly, do not entirely conform to the classical standards of Western liberal democracies. It is doubtful that Kim Jong Un, Alexander Lukashenko or, say, Mohammed bin Salman, or even Donald Trump, would suddenly decide to offer Vladimir Putin wise advice on how to organise polling stations properly and count votes.

It is hardly likely that the Kremlin felt an urgent need to erect elaborate and expensive but not especially durable scenery on the Russian political stage when the reaction of the potential audience to the forthcoming theatrical production was known in advance. It seems more logical to assume that the Russian authorities need elections not as cosmetic decoration for the façade of their political system, designed to attract the indifferent gaze of an outside observer, but as a quite effective and, above all, much-needed mechanism for maintaining dialogue between the authorities and society in the difficult geopolitical and socio-economic conditions of autumn 2026.

First and foremost, the Russian authorities are fighting hard for a high turnout, creating the most comfortable possible conditions for their voters to cast their ballots. This is no accident. A high turnout is convincing evidence of the population’s continued political activity and of the fact that Russian society has not descended into political apathy and wholesale cynicism. The idea of active civic participation is far from an empty phrase for the country’s leadership. In this sense, even a vote against the main “party of power”, United Russia, is clearly preferable to the alternative of a significant part of the electorate conspicuously choosing not to participate in the elections.

No less important, the authorities need the election results as a barometer of current public preferences, something even the most accurate opinion polls or in-depth sociological research cannot replace. Contemporary Russia undoubtedly has its own, albeit relatively narrow, political spectrum of “systemic opposition” parties reflecting the differing interests and expectations of various social, economic, age and regional groups. The constantly changing balance of power between these parties must, one way or another, be taken into account by the authorities when determining the future priorities of their strategy.

For example, relative success for the Communist Party, A Just Russia and candidates from other left-wing parties would be a signal that the authorities should pay more attention to social programmes, the fight against economic inequality and social polarisation, and to countering the many remnants of “wild capitalism” left over from the 1990s. Conversely, a large number of votes cast for the New People party and other right-wing candidates would provide grounds for accelerating structural economic reforms and creating additional opportunities for the private sector, including small and medium-sized businesses. Strong electoral results for the Liberal Democratic Party would indicate growing nationalist tendencies in Russian society. The authorities may respond to such political signals in different ways, but they cannot ignore them and must therefore read shifts in public sentiment correctly.

Moreover, it can be assumed with a considerable degree of confidence that the State Duma elections will, one way or another, lead to substantial changes in the composition of not only the lower house of the Russian parliament but also Russia’s federal government. Following the elections, significant personnel changes are likely to take place in the executive branch – both at the federal level and at other levels. Such personnel changes, in turn, will make room for fresh ideas, innovative programmes, unconventional projects and proposals. There is a clear demand for renewal in Russian society today. Parliamentary elections are one way of responding convincingly to this demand without calling into question the stability of the state’s overall strategy or its senior leadership.

The Duma elections are the first parliamentary elections held during the special military operation, during which Russian society has changed considerably. In a sense, they can be called a large-scale political experiment whose outcome remains difficult to predict with precision. For example, it is still difficult to determine with confidence which political force will be supported by the majority of people who have participated in the special military operation or who remain on the line of contact. No less uncertainty remains regarding the likely political preferences of many residents of the new Russian regions, for whom the September elections will be their first State Duma election in their new status.

Such an experiment probably carries a degree of risk for the Russian leadership. Nevertheless, the leadership appears prepared to take that risk, not without reason viewing elections not only as an important but as an indispensable mechanism for public confirmation of its continuing political legitimacy.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: India’s hollow political parties can’t a make solid democracy
editorials.passage:
High drama erupted in the small hours of a suspense-filled January day in Kolkata. Masked officers of the Enforcement Directorate swept into the glossy offices of I-PAC (Indian Political Action Committee), one of the country’s leading political consultancies.

They hauled away computers and files as the stunned staff looked on. Mamata Banerjee, then the Bengal chief minister and leader of the state’s governing party, rushed to the scene and walked out with several files. She complained to the reporters at the site that the “politically motivated” raid was being orchestrated by Delhi to steal information on her Trinamool Congress party’s election strategy and potential candidate lists for the 2026 state Assembly elections scheduled later in the year.

Television channels played on loop the drama of one mystery-filled “ green file ” she had walked out with, in this latest episode of Banerjee’s running battles with the Centre.

It was only the beginning of I-PAC’s woes – and Banerjee’s – as the Bharatiya Janata Party dispensation in the Centre was closing in on her. It unleashed federal probe and regulatory agencies like the Enforcement Directorate and the Central Bureau of Investigation to break her aides and financiers, flew in top BJP leaders and ace workers for the campaign, and poured money like water for the April election. Simultaneously, through the Special Intensive Revision under a pliant Election Commission, it made sure that the state’s 27% Muslims – who used to rally behind Banerjee fearing the BJP’s Hindu supremacist politics – were strategically whittled down in the electoral list.

The war on I-PAC was a surgical strike on the Trinamool Congress’s campaign machine delivered on top of these multiple strategies to break Banerjee’s 15-year grip on power in Bengal. A few months later, the Enforcement Directorate would arrest I-PAC’s co-founder and director on a money laundering case just two weeks before the election in April.

Narendra Modi eventually got what he wanted, and the BJP won a landslide with a two-thirds majority in the state Assembly, his strategies of vote capture complemented by the strong undercurrent of aversion for Banerjee’s party for its pervading corruption and thuggery. Job done, the I-PAC director was released on bail by a court the very day after the state election concluded. The Enforcement Directorate did not even oppose the bail in court this time.

Thus ended the reign of Banerjee whose supposedly well-knit grass-roots organisation almost made her invincible, till she wasn’t. It would seem odd that a consulting firm would be so central to a political party with what looked like a high level of organisational coherence. But it presents a stark reality of the deepening global recession of democracy: the professionalisation of politics with the withering of mass political parties.

As foundational institutions of democratic governance, political parties worldwide are experiencing organisational decay and popular disengagement, eroding their capacity for connecting citizens to the state and political processes.

As parties are becoming ever more dependent on big money while grass-roots party organisations such as unions and associations decline as primary sources of funding and mobilisation, political accountability shifts from party constituents to shadowy patrons and technocrats. And politics increasingly moves from volunteer-driven social activism to specialised, expert-managed campaigns driven by data analytics, public relations strategies and digital marketing. Political consultancies are the key in mediating this transition.

They provide voter databases, targeted messaging strategies, ground‑level micro‑campaigning and organisational planning – functions that would once be considered the domain of political parties but which are now too incapacitated to perform these themselves. Consultancies even find and rent crowds to attend rallies to help parties and leaders project popularity.

In this managerialisation of politics, corporate management ideologies, techniques, and values replace ideological contestation and elections come to resemble corporate marketing campaigns rather than battles of ideas. Nothing screams crisis of democracy louder than political parties having to pay consultants to tell them what voters want.

Political consultancies have now become an integral part of India’s party politics. Most parties not only work with consultants, they have also themselves created in-house consultancy-like wings staffed with professionals, often drawn from consulting firms.

In December 2022, police in Hyderabad raided the office of a consulting firm handling the Telangana Congress’s “ war room ”. They were clearly doing a great job – the Congress came to power in Telangana within a year. The Trinamool Congress, which also created an in-house consultancy, similarly came to depend on I-PAC to provide it the party’s technical core that made the crackdown such a crippling blow.

It was the 2014 general election that marked the beginning of the rise of political consultancies in a major way. Modi himself benefited hugely from a professionalised campaign modelled on the US presidential strategies, primarily focusing on the person of the candidate rather than the party’s programmes.

The pioneering consultancy co-founded by political strategist Prashant Kishor that managed Modi’s campaign revolutionised Indian elections with data-driven outreach, voter analytics, booth-level mapping and social media drive; Kishor’s team later evolved into I-PAC that was consulting Banerjee.

In a country with poor campaign finance laws, this managerial invasion of politics has grave cost implications for campaigns, and in turn, for its democracy. Indian elections are now among the costliest in the world. In India’s 2019 general election, campaign spending reached $7.2 billion surpassing the $6.5 billion spent in the 2016 US presidential and congressional elections put together – despite India’s per capita income being just 3% of that of the United States.

Election campaigns were never cheap, but when professional managers and specialists replace voluntary political workers, somebody has to foot the additional bill. With the decline of traditional sources of party funds such as trade unions and membership subscriptions, parties have become even more dependent on business fat cats to meet the rising expenses.

This not only makes parties more accountable to financial patrons than their constituencies, it also tilts the balance decisively in favour of politicians with access to pots of money, affecting the quality of representation. Elite capture is exacerbated, adding to the already debilitating pathologies of poor internal democracy that has long characterised the institutional weakening of Indian political parties.

Party deficiencies such as the absence of mobilising organisations embedded in society have contributed to the distancing between people and political parties that lies at the core of the worldwide loss of public trust in politicians and governments. It is manifested in Gen Z movements from Madagascar to Nepal, and most recently in India itself, where a meme-inspired “cockroach movement” against the country’s broken public examination system forced Modi to accept the resignation of his education minister. Gen Z movements have thus stepped into the void left by hollow parties.

In The Hollow Parties: The Many Pasts and Disordered Present of American Party Politics , Daniel Schlozman and Sam Rosenfeld describe US political parties as hard shells lacking internal cohesion and positive loyalties, failing to link citizens to governments or build governing coalitions. The book traces this hollowness through over 200 years and concludes that party weakening in the US accelerated since the 1970s, when external groups started filling the void in the political parties. This happened as the Vietnam war, stagflation, and the 1960s civil rights revolution ended the union-boosting New Deal order of regulated capitalism and welfare expansion that once helped mass parties thrive.

Political consultancies, pressure groups like Political Action Committees and think-tanks emerged to fill the void as political reforms in the US made nominations and funding more participatory but weakened party gatekeeping. By the 1990s, political consultants were handling polling, media, and voter targeting – tasks once handled by parties. They grew into a billion-dollar industry, which simply exploded after 2010 when the US Supreme Court removed all legal limits on independent political spending. In India, political consultancies began to boom soon after, replicating the model in the US.

The corporatisation of political parties has the effect of accentuating an old pathology of democratic politics: the tendency towards elitism. Modern democracy, as argued by thinkers like Joseph Schumpeter and Robert Michels, is essentially controlled by a small elite group even if it allows for mass participation. Corporatisation of politics intensifies the process. As greater professionalisation of politics necessitates more financial resources to wage campaigns, democratic elitism deepens.

Power becomes more concentrated among a small, privileged group with wealth and connections helping them to gain primacy and leverage over the grass-roots. Power also becomes stickier as access to power increases a party’s ability to afford technocratic avenues of retaining power, such as the services offered by political consultancies. Power begets money, and money begets power.

Noticeably in India, since Modi’s rise to national power in 2014, the turnover rates in governments, both at federal and state levels, have dropped sharply. The electoral outcome in Bengal ending Banerjee’s reign is one of the few exceptions to this rule but the scale of the challenge mounted against her regional party could only have been pulled off by a party like the BJP that has access to power, and hence the resources; Modi’s party now gets 10 times the corporate donations received by all other national parties put together. The traditionally strong parties in Bengal, namely the Congress and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) that have ruled the state in the past and still have a fair bit of organisational presence, could not have remotely matched either the Trinamool Congress’s or the BJP’s campaign. Lack of power and money can spell political death in this post-political, technocratic world of politics.

Banerjee’s party, now stripped of state power and the associated access to business funding minted on the ability to dispense state favours, joins this vast landscape of zombies. Within days of her party’s defeat, it began to collapse like a house of cards. The majority of her 80 MLAs have joined a rebel faction, while 20 of the 28 of her MPs merged with a little-known party. Having lost control over the legislative wing of the party, Banerjee is now at the very real risk of losing the registered name and symbol of the party that she built from scratch.

The unravelling of the Trinamool Congress again shows the ability of technocracy in surrogating power in hollowed out parties. Its dependence on the managerial expertise of a consultant is hardly a surprise in retrospect. If Banerjee’s Trinamool Congress had a semblance of the social-movement qualities or ideological and organisational coherence that bind together parties, it would have been impossible to disintegrate at the pace it has. Absent all of these, it was held together by what the Russians call “ politicheskya tekhnologiya” , or political technology . It is the engineering of politics that fills polities with zombie parties rolling on dark money and dark structures with no ideological or programmatic coherence.

In countries like India, where electoral funding is highly opaque and political donations are tax-exempt, parties are also prime sites of political technology through their role in money laundering and deal-making rather than as vehicles of social change. An extreme form of this is registered unrecognised political parties, which fail the minimum threshold of vote share and seats to be recognised as political parties but cannot be legally de-registered.

The unknown party that Banerjee’s Trinamool Congress rebels merged with was a registered unrecognised political parties called the Nationalist Citizens Party of India, which contested in all of three seats in Tripura’s last state election and its best performer garnered just 536 votes. There are over 3,200 such zombie parties that received more than Rs 10,000 crore in electoral donations in two years from 2022 to 2024, pulling in more than the BJP and the Congress even though they barely participate in elections.

Democracy is supposed to be about popular demand, but political technology, which spans everything from manipulating the news agenda to seeding proxy parties and dummy political organisations, engineers the political system from the supply side with the help of consultants and other variants of political technologists. In “ Political Technology: The Globalisation of Political Manipulation ”, Andrew Wilson writes that political technology helps explain “the speed of democratic deterioration in previously stable liberal democracies…Democracy has lost power to technocracy.”

This technocratic churn makes parties hollower, the political playing field uneven, political contestation unfair, and democracy weaker. The professionalisation of politics that replaces ideological contests also hollows out party identity. Big-tent parties begin to resemble one another and their programmatic differences begin to lose practical salience. Politics begins to resemble a marketing war between different sets of elites. Public trust in conventional parties erodes as politics looks performative and detached from ordinary life and voters look for authenticity, even it is to be found in the extremities. Like, the virtually indistinguishable Tories and Labour are driving voters towards Reform and the Greens in the UK.

The unqualified malice of polarisation’s “us versus them” appeal is an easy foil to this technocracy-mediated political ambiguity of hollow parties. Polarisation helps differentiate a distinct ideological brand in an anodyne political space. The rabid Hindu supremacism of Modi’s BJP affords it a clear brand advantage in a crowded field of parties mouthing the same homilies of development, welfare and governance.

Its distinct ideological appeal combined with its incremental capture of governing institutions and the backing of Big Money makes the BJP a juggernaut on a roll. A rudderless opposition struggling with the universal pathologies enervating conventional parties everywhere offers no roadblock. If anything, they smoothen its ride.

Hollowed out political parties offer little resistance to authoritarian encroachment because when parties lose organisational strength, the opposition becomes easier to sideline, reducing the possibility that abuses of power will be checked before they metastasise into a new regime. Without organised parties, civil society pushbacks lose sting as such pressures lack a durable route to state power, helping authoritarian actors consolidate. Like, the recent Gen Z “cockroach movement” may have dimmed Modi’s aura, but is unlikely to dent his power.

Without translation into political change, policy, or institutional reform, which is only possible through political parties, the energy of such mass movements can dissipate. Which increasingly appears to be the case as hollowed out opposition parties are in no state to act on the opening created by the success of the cockroach movement.

In his seminal book, “ Ruling the Void: The Hollowing of Western Democracy” , Peter Mair argues that as political parties stop functioning as social organisations, they become more appendages of the state than society. Stability becomes more their thing rather than disruptive political movements. Wedded to the state and Big Money, India’s hollow parties increasingly manifest these pathologies.

When a fully captured Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision last year in Bihar, the opposition parties first launched protests alleging it was a ploy to manipulate voter lists to steal elections. Then, they went on to participate in, and validate, the same election rather than boycott it. The SIR has been rolled out nationwide since, shaving off roughly a tenth of the electorate and helping Modi’s party pull off incredible wins, like in Bengal, without much substantive resistance from the opposition parties.

India’s political parties thus hold important lessons for global democratic decay. Parties are central to democratic politics but are often overlooked in the analyses of degrading democracies, yet democratic politics cannot be bolstered without addressing the pathologies of the political parties that lie at the heart of it. As the Indian case shows, hollow parties can’t make solid democracies.

Much of the contemporary understanding of democratic erosion rests on institution capture (or, supply-side backsliding), the rising inequality and the associated resentments paving the way for demagogues (demand-side), and distortions of intermediary institutions like the media. The supply-side analyses mostly deal with governing institutions such as the legislatures and the courts, which modern despots capture and systematically hollow out. But that is not the only way democracies go bad. As the Indian case shows, they also begin to rot when political parties lose the vitality to act as a countervailing force against totalising power. And, open the gates to cockroaches.

Debasish Roy Chowdhury is a journalist, researcher and author based in Hong Kong, having recently co-authored To Kill a Democracy: India’s Passage to Despotism, OUP/Pan Macmillan.

A longer version of this article first appeared on the Toda Peace Institute website .

editorials.title: Why do the forever friends of our 20s become strangers in our 30s?
editorials.passage:
I can name 11 cities I have lived in, but not even half the people who made them liveable.

Somewhere in a drawer is an old SIM card with 200 phone numbers, and all I remember are names or just faces. Sometimes a vague detail surfaces: the flatmate who ate the crust of the bread first; the friend who could not sleep without the fan on, even in December, and who once made me sit through three hours of a film he loved; the friend who knew every bus route in a city I have not returned to in nine years.

In your 20s, everyone you meet seems like a permanent friend, when proximity feels like intimacy and frequency gets mistaken for love. There is that person one sees every day, whose voice you would recognise through a wall, whose kitchen you know better than your own; surely, that is the kind of life-long sentence, a good one. Surely, such a person cannot vanish from your life.

Yet, they do, and mostly without any drama.

I lost people to time, which is the ordinary way. Some I lost to death, ordinary when you’re older but unbearable when you’re younger. Some I lost to plain uncertainty: an illness, a marriage that swallowed them whole, a visa refused, a phone number that stopped working and was never replaced with another.

Some I lost to politics, unexpectedly. One assumes affection could hold the weight of disagreement. It turns out that for some you can be a friend of 15 years right up until the evening you are not: an argument built up over dinner as I heard myself sounding faster and surer while he got quieter. At the door, we said goodbye and I stood there while he walked to his car, and I went back in and cleared the plates.

Some were lost to distance as I moved a city, then another, and suddenly there came a border, a change in my field of work and a life – moving does the work that an argument might have. Distance grows over time, becoming noticeable over the years as correspondence dwindles to birthdays and then nothing – all quite painlessly.

I look at their lives from the outside, like gazing into a window from the street. They have the same five people they have always had. The five have become 10 with spouses and 15 with children. They holiday together. They have inside jokes and probably a group chat I am not in and would not know what to say if I were.

I am not missed, nor do I want to be. I was not there for the hospital visits, the house moving, or the bad years. You cannot be absent for the substance of a life and then expect to be present in its accounting. I have a life, a good one. It has almost none of the people I once knew as indispensable. I do not know what to do with that.

At 33, you stop blaming distance and geography and start doing an audit.

I lost friends because I was short-tempered, too much, too loud in the room, too insistent, and too quick to turn an evening into an argument I had to win. I lost people because I was too little, because I did not call, because I let three months become a year for no defensible reason.

I lost people because I drank too much.

I lost people because I read too much, bringing my thoughts into rooms where nobody had asked for them. I lost people because I had travelled and they had not. I lost people because I had not travelled enough, and they had.

Some of that is remorse. But what I have arrived at provisionally is that friendship is a shared present that lasts as long as two people occupy the same stretch of time together. When that stops, the friendship fades into completion. We are the ones who insist on reading completion as failure, because we were taught that only the permanent counts.

I no longer think permanence is the measure.

I have a life, a good one. It has almost none of the people I once knew as indispensable. On the days I can carry this lightly, it seems like evidence that I was loved in 11 cities, briefly and sufficiently, by people who have gone on to be loved elsewhere. Other days I open the drawer and look at the SIM card, and I cannot remember a single name.

Pranav Sharma is a historian of science who lives and writes from New Delhi, India and Paro, Bhutan.

editorials.title: Did Pakistan create a false-flag naval collision to provoke India and weasel out of Mecca pact commitments?
editorials.passage:
Does the Mecca pact have anything to do with a Pakistani corvette deliberately colliding with an Indian warship in international waters on Tuesday evening? It may sound implausible, but there might be a strong connection.

Before I expand on that, it might be worth looking at what the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, or the Mecca pact, between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan stands for. Modelled on Nato’s Article 5, the pact holds that an armed attack against any one of the three member states will be considered an attack against all of them.

The agreement, at least theoretically, seeks to harness Saudi Arabia’s financial muscle, Turkey’s drone manufacturing capabilities and Pakistan’s nuclear-armed military. The pact, however, lacks any enforcement mechanism or joint command structure.

In reality, the Mecca pact serves different purposes for different members. For the Saudis, it is primarily a contingency plan, a hedge against America’s growing unpredictability and Riyadh’s inability to trust Washington as a reliable security guarantor.

Faced with threats posed by Iran and its proxy networks, and lacking a battle-hardened military to deter regional adversaries, the Kingdom, despite its massive financial resources, suffers from a deep strategic vulnerability.

This is the core motivation behind Riyadh’s stitching together of alternative security arrangements to protect its vital energy exports. Saudi Arabia signed a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Pakistan last year and upgraded it to the Mecca pact with the addition of Turkey this year. The pact reflects increasing Saudi attempts to avoid relying on the US for its national security.

Pakistan is a different kettle of fish. Islamabad sees the pact primarily as a deterrence mechanism against India. The Iran-aligned Houthis might be threatening Saudi oil exports and energy infrastructure, but Pakistan, despite the collective security pledge of the trilateral pact, sees no reason for intervention or mobilisation of its military for an anti-insurgency operation in West Asia.

All that Shehbaz Sharif has offered so far is a condemnation of the “dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack against the Holy Site of Makkah Al-Mukarramah” without naming the Houthis or their chief patron, the Iranians.

While the Pakistani defence minister has paid lip service to pact commitments, the all-powerful military’s spokesperson has told Al Arabiya English that the defence pact had “no aggressive element” and was based on “collective deterrence”, terming it “purely defensive”.

Pakistan went into the pact because it needed an insurance policy against Indian military assertiveness and the change in force posture after the Pahalgam terror attack. The killing of 26 Indian civilians by Pakistani terrorists caused India to launch Operation Sindoor and declare that any major terrorist attack on Indian soil henceforth will be treated as an act of war, eliminating any distinction between the actual terrorists and their state sponsors.

India also explicitly rejected Pakistan’s nuclear blackmail as a deterrent against countermeasures and said that it was reserving the right to execute precise, decisive strikes inside hostile territory. The Pakistani response has been to leverage the West Asian security architecture to fortify its eastern flank.

It was never Islamabad’s intention to honour the pact — especially by fighting the Houthis in West Asia — and get dragged headlong into an asymmetric regional quagmire. Additionally, Pakistani military action against the Houthis would mean locking horns with Iran. Islamabad isn’t looking forward to making an enemy out of a confident Tehran, more so as it shares a 900 km border that runs through the restive Balochistan province. With Pakistan’s military already stretched thin managing a volatile Afghan border, inviting Iranian retaliation is a strategic non-starter.

Pakistan’s reluctance is also anchored in its domestic vulnerabilities. Home to a massive Shia population, with representation even among the military officer corps, any involvement against an Iran-backed Shia militia might be uncomfortable and viewed through a sectarian lens at home. So, Pakistan’s reluctance to come to the aid of the Saudis is also an attempt to avoid inflaming domestic fault lines.
It has refused Saudi requests for deployment before. In early 2015, Saudi Arabia officially asked Pakistan to supply ground troops, warships and combat aircraft to join Operation Decisive Storm against the Houthi forces. Then Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif referred the decision to Pakistan’s Parliament. On April 10, 2015, after a week-long debate, the Pakistani parliament unanimously passed a resolution mandating that Pakistan maintain neutrality in Yemen.

Lawmakers had pledged that Pakistan would defend Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and holy sites if invaded, but drew a hard line against deploying forces inside Yemen, causing diplomatic friction with Riyadh.
Islamabad is willing to deploy troops in stationary, defensive roles within Saudi borders to keep the passage of financial bailouts well lubricated, but it has scrambled to define the alliance as strictly defensive, with no broader regional aspirations.

Therefore, when the Saudis, running low on missile interceptors, approached Western and regional allies such as France, Britain and Egypt, as well as partner Pakistan, for air defence support against missiles and loitering munitions, Pakistan had to devise a way to dodge its obligations without appearing to betray Riyadh.
What Islamabad needed, more than anything else, was a false-flag operation that would create a distraction and turn the focus away from the fact that it isn’t willing to honour the commitments of the Mecca pact. Under these circumstances, Pakistan attempted to do what it has done before: trigger a conflict with India.

The recent incident in the north Arabian Sea, when a Pakistani corvette, PNS Hunain, collided with an Indian Navy warship approximately 220 kilometres east of Oman, might have been an attempt at a calculated provocation.

India summoned the Pakistani envoy and lodged a strong protest, while the Ministry of External Affairs, in a statement, said that though the “incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991.”

The agreement explicitly prohibits naval vessels from engaging in provocative actions or approaching one another with hostile intent. Media reports, such as one in Hindustan Times quoting an unnamed MEA official, said the “episode involved a close-in manoeuvring by the Pakistani vessel, which approached the Indian warship at high speed and in an unsafe manner” after shadowing the Indian vessel and ignoring repeated warnings.

Times of India quoted another source as saying, “Even under extreme provocation, the Indian warship’s captain exercised extreme restraint”, while the Pakistani vessel returned after suffering “severe damage”.

It is worth noting that despite the gravity of the breach of the agreement and the dangerous manoeuvre, the Indian side responded with responsibility and restraint, effectively denying Pakistan the geopolitical flare-up it appeared to be seeking.
A military escalation with India would have fundamentally altered the prevailing stability, providing Islamabad with a plausible force majeure argument. Had India retaliated forcefully, Pakistan would have got an opportunity to cite a ‘threat to national security’ to override treaty obligations with the Saudis.

This chicanery conforms to a recurring pattern in Pakistan’s behaviour. There exists a serious, scholarly hypothesis on how Pakistan, in 2001, orchestrated the terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament to weasel its way out of American pressure to take action against fleeing al-Qaeda terrorists post-9/11.

In December 2001, the US and its allies had Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda operatives cornered in the Tora Bora mountains of eastern Afghanistan. They were left with only one escape route — crossing the porous border into the unregulated tribal regions of Pakistan. Washington put the Pakistani military under immense pressure to deploy troops and seal the border.

That presented Pakistan’s powerful intelligence agency, the ISI, with a dilemma. Intercepting fleeing al-Qaeda leaders would spark domestic blowback and turn the terrorist network against the Pakistani state. The ISI needed an escape hatch.
The audacious December 13, 2001, terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament was carried out by terrorists from Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) cells under ISI guidance. Weapons and instructions came from Pakistan, investigations revealed. Phone records pointed to handlers in Karachi and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. The operation was designed to elicit a severe Indian response. Expectedly, New Delhi launched Operation Parakram — the largest military mobilisation in Indian history along the LoC.

Pakistan, in retaliation, moved the bulk of the 11th and 12th Corps — the formations the George W. Bush administration had just asked it to put on the Afghan frontier to catch al-Qaeda operatives fleeing Tora Bora — east towards India.

Stimson Center researchers note: “As India mobilized forces, Pakistan responded in kind. Despite US pleas and protests, Pakistan in late December (2001) began redeploying to its borders with India most of the 11th and 12th Army Corps sent to the border with Afghanistan only a month earlier, at Washington’s urging. Pakistan left in place two brigades, or about 6,000 of these regular troops to help seal the Afghan border. Most US policymakers believe that the redeployment of the better equipped, more capable Pakistan Army regulars undercut whatever possibility existed of halting the passage of fleeing al-Queda and Taliban operatives.”

Then CIA Islamabad station chief Robert Grenier and US ambassador to Pakistan Wendy Chamberlin suspected the ISI had approved the Parliament attack so that Pakistani forces would be pulled off the border, opening a path for bin Laden. In their critically acclaimed book The Exile: The Flight of Osama bin Laden, investigative journalists Cathy Scott-Clark and Adrian Levy quote Grenier as wondering whether JeM could have hit Parliament without ISI knowledge and whether the timing was “a deliberate ruse”.

Bruce Riedel, a former CIA officer and a National Security Council staffer at the Bush White House in 2001, in an op-ed for the Brookings Institution written in 2008, mused: “I asked myself then and still do: who benefited from this attack? The answer is the JeM’s friend and ally, Osama bin Laden’s al-Qaeda. In December 2001, al-Qaeda was on the run, even on the ropes. The US and allied forces had overthrown the Taliban Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan in a lightning operation. (Gen Pervez) Musharraf had switched sides, at least for the time, and reversed a decade of Pakistani support for the Taliban and was promising Washington that he would help catch bin Laden and the rest of the fleeing al-Qaeda gang… By diverting Pakistan’s army to the east, to the border with India for the next year, the Parliament attack helped save al-Qaeda.”

By triggering a near-war scenario with India, Pakistan managed to thwart American pressure and preserve its jihadist links and assets. It is possible that a similar dirty trick was attempted this week in international waters to heighten tensions with India so that Islamabad may feign helplessness before the Saudis. India’s restraint poured cold water on the hot plan. It would be interesting to observe the fate of the Mecca pact from here.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: PISA scores are falling: Are today’s students less capable in the AI age?
editorials.passage:
The latest PISA results have stoked the familiar flames of anguish. They show that school-going teenagers are losing their grip on reading, mathematics and science.
For those unfamiliar with PISA, the Programme for International Student Assessment is an international assessment by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that tests 15-year-olds across participating countries, usually every three years. The 2025 assessment was the ninth PISA cycle, covering 91 countries and more than 760,000 students. Students are evaluated on how well they can apply reading, mathematics and science knowledge to solve real-world problems.
The 2025 results, released on September 8, show that student performance across OECD countries has fallen to its lowest recorded level. Reading scores dropped 28 points between 2015 and 2025, equivalent to roughly one and a half years of learning. Mathematics fell by 22 points, while science remained relatively stable, though still concerning.
The explanation is already familiar: too much screen time, less reading for pleasure and constant digital distraction. The share of "hasty readers" — students who answer quickly but incorrectly — has also risen sharply since 2018.
Although India is not part of the OECD’s PISA comparison, the findings broadly echo concerns here too. Excessive screen usage, changing reading habits and uneven access to digital learning may be reshaping how students learn across geographies.
As a parent of a school-going teenager in India, I’m rather puzzled by the other possibilities at play here. Are we measuring students right in the age of AI? Are we interpreting the cognitive ability of a new generation through the mental model of an older one?
Calling an entire generation "less capable" deserves more scrutiny.

The conflict
A 2023 Oxford Internet Institute study of nearly 12,000 American children aged 9 to 12 found no meaningful link between screen time and measures of cognitive or mental well-being, even among children with relatively high digital engagement. This does not mean digital habits are harmless. But it does challenge the easy assumption that more screen time automatically produces less capable minds. That causal link has become common in public debate without equally strong evidence.
Longer-term research raises another question. IQ scores rose steadily through much of the 20th century, a trend known as the Flynn Effect. But scores later levelled off and declined in several Northern European countries from around the 1990s. This happened before smartphones became widespread. Something has therefore been changing in standardised measures of cognitive performance for longer than today's debate about screens and social media suggests. The causes may be more complicated than simply blaming ubiquitous digital technology.

When the test meets a different world
PISA was created for a world in which information was relatively scarce. Books, classrooms, and libraries were the main gateways to knowledge. Showing that you were competent often meant remembering information and using it through sustained reasoning.
That world has not disappeared. But it is no longer the only world in which today's teenagers live and learn.
A digitally native teenager lives in an environment of absurd information abundance. AI chatbots and search engines provide answers in seconds. Videos can explain ideas that once required several pages of a textbook and a tutor. AI can now draft, summarise, critique and suggest answers almost instantly.
What looks like distraction in a PISA test may sometimes be an adaptation to an environment that the test was not designed to measure.
Scrolling through 50 pieces of information in five minutes does not mean understanding them. Finding information quickly is not the same as knowing what it means. Careful reading, persistence, evaluation and reflection still matter.
The real question is not whether these skills have become obsolete. They have not. It is whether they are being weakened - to the extent of non-functionality - as digital habits become more deeply embedded in everyday life.

Students are learning for two worlds
PISA 2025 did not simply repeat its existing tests. For the first time, it included an assessment called "Learning in the Digital World", which looked at how students solve complex problems using digital tools.
Almost two-thirds of OECD students reached the relevant level in computational problem-solving. But another finding is more revealing: only about half were proficient in both digital problem-solving and basic reading and mathematics.
This points to the central education problem of the moment.
Some students may be developing skills for both worlds. Others may be gaining digital fluency while losing ground in basic literacy and numeracy. We still do not know whether digital competence can compensate for weaker foundational skills in real-world performance. There is no long-term evidence strong enough to say that it can. Educators should therefore be careful about assuming that it will.
The evidence points to two trends happening at the same time. Basic skills are declining, and that decline is concerning. At the same time, new digital abilities are emerging, allowing the individual to adapt to the environment. What remains unclear is how these new abilities relate to the skills they may be replacing.
The bigger question is therefore not simply whether today's teenagers are getting smarter or less capable. It is whether they are becoming capable in ways that match the world they are entering, and whether some weaknesses will only become visible much later, if at all.

What counts as intelligence or competence?
Throughout human history, societies have defined intelligence or competence according to the demands of their prevailing conditions. What counted as appropriate in an agrarian society was different from what mattered in an industrial one. The digital age is changing that reorganization again, and AI is accelerating the shift to everyone's discomfort.
Digital habits that look like fragmented attention may sometimes be a form of rapid navigation through an information environment that earlier generations never experienced at this scale. We should be careful not to mistake unfamiliarity for cognitive or intellectual weakness.
The PISA results tell us that some foundational abilities are weakening. We need to take that seriously even as we recognise that students are developing new digital capabilities.

The task for schools
This makes the task for education harder, not easier.
Schools must continue to teach foundational knowledge and deep reasoning. These abilities do not become optional simply because technology has become more powerful. At the same time, education needs better ways to identify and measure new skills, such as, evaluating information from multiple sources, working with AI and exercising judgement when technology provides plausible answers. We do not yet have sufficiently tested ways of measuring many of these abilities. That is a gap in our education systems.
The real challenge is therefore not to force a digitally native generation back into the cognitive habits of an analogue age. Nor should we romanticise every habit produced by the digital world. We need to find out, with humility, which old capabilities remain essential, which new ones are genuinely emerging, and whether the two strengthen each other or substitute for each other. That may also require a broader conception of knowledge, skills, and competence suited for the emerging hyper-digitised world.
That is ultimately an empirical question, not a battle between old and new values. The answer will not come from nostalgia for the past or optimism about technology. It will require education systems to measure, honestly and rigorously, what today's students are gaining, what they are losing and what capabilities they will actually need in the world ahead.
The next generation may not be thinking less or be less capable.
They may simply be adapting in a world we did not design for them.



(Sreejith Sreedharan is a technology analyst and author of ‘Future of Work – AI Augmented Autonomous Decentralised’. He works on organisational AI readiness and created the AI Instinct Index®, a psychometric diagnostic designed to assess behavioural readiness for AI adoption and adaptive capacity in constraint-heavy environments.
